title: DSA Curriculum
subtitle: Every problem in the library, in the order that teaches it.
intro:
This is the problem bank with a **spine**. The same problems, the same judge —
but arranged as a course that starts at `System.out.println` and ends at
tries, Dijkstra and 2-D dynamic programming.

**How to use it.** Work top to bottom. Open a unit, read *Why this exists* and
*The model*, copy the skeleton out by hand once, then climb the rungs. A rung
is a group of problems that drill the same twist; when a rung stops being
interesting, move on — you do not have to clear every problem to progress.

**What "done" means here.** A unit turns green when you have solved most of its
core rungs, but the number is not the point: the point is that when you next
read a prompt with the words *"contiguous subarray"* in it, your hands start
typing a sliding window before you have finished the sentence. The **Signals**
table in each unit is that reflex, written down.

**Where the depth is.** Each unit links the full lesson for its technique in
**Learn** — that is where the derivations, the worked examples and the
language-level detail live. The unit page is the map; Learn is the terrain.

stages.title: Foundations
stages.tagline: Make the keyboard stop being the bottleneck.
stages.goal:
Before a single algorithm is worth learning, four things have to be automatic:
reading input, doing arithmetic without overflowing, branching, and looping.
Every problem in this stage is solvable in under ten lines. That is the point —
you are not learning to think yet, you are learning to type what you already
think without stopping to look anything up.

Finish this stage when you can open any of its problems and have a correct
program before you have finished re-reading the statement.

units.title: Input, Output & Arithmetic
units.tagline: Read the numbers, do the sum, print the answer.
units.why:
Every problem in this app speaks one protocol: the grader writes your input to
**stdin**, your program writes its answer to **stdout**, and the two are
compared as text. No function is called for you and nothing is returned. Until
that loop is automatic — read, compute, print — every other idea in the
curriculum is blocked behind a plumbing problem.

This unit also introduces the first bug that will follow you all the way to the
Hard problems: an `int` in Java holds numbers up to about 2.1 billion, and
quietly wraps around past that.
units.model:
### The shape of every program here

```
read the input  →  compute  →  print exactly one answer
```

**Reading.** `Scanner` is the readable choice and fast enough for everything in
this stage. `sc.nextInt()` pulls the next whitespace-separated token and parses
it; `sc.nextLine()` takes the rest of the current line, newline included.
Whitespace — spaces versus newlines — does not matter to `nextInt()`, which is
why problem statements can describe input loosely.

**Printing.** `System.out.println(x)` writes the value and a newline. The judge
normalises trailing whitespace and trailing blank lines, so a stray final
newline will not fail you — but a missing digit, an extra word, or different
capitalisation will.

**Arithmetic on `int`.** `/` between two `int`s is *integer division*: it
truncates toward zero, so `7 / 2` is `3` and `-7 / 2` is `-3`. `%` is the
remainder and keeps the sign of the left operand, so `-7 % 3` is `-1`, not `2`.
Both facts will bite you in the digits unit.

**Overflow.** `int` spans −2,147,483,648 … 2,147,483,647. Multiply two values
near 100,000 and you are already outside it — silently, with a wrong answer
rather than a crash. When a constraint says values reach 10⁹, or when you
multiply or sum many of them, compute in `long`.

signals.why: Nothing to read; the whole program is one `println`.

signals.when: “A single integer n” / “two integers a and b”
signals.why: Order in the statement is order on the input.
Text can contain spaces, so tokens are the wrong unit.

signals.when: Constraints reach 10⁹, or you multiply two inputs
signals.why: Two values near 10⁹ overflow `int` on the very first multiply.

skeletons.name: Read numbers, print an answer
skeletons.when: The default shape for almost every problem in the app.
skeletons.note: Declare `Scanner` once, read in statement order, print exactly one line.

skeletons.name: Read a whole line of text
skeletons.when: When the input is a sentence, a word, or anything with spaces.
skeletons.note: Mixing `nextInt()` and `nextLine()` needs care — see the pitfalls.

skeletons.name: Compute in long, print as long
skeletons.when: Any time a product or a running sum can leave int's range.
skeletons.note: `(long) a * b` casts *before* multiplying; `(long)(a * b)` is already too late.

traces.title: What Java actually computes
traces.intro: Arithmetic has no loop to step through, but it does have state: the *type* of each intermediate result. Read the expression, predict the value, then check the row.
rows: Both operands are `int`, so the fraction is discarded.
Truncates toward **zero**, not down — Python's `//` would give −4.
The remainder takes the sign of the dividend.
Always in `[0, 2)` — what you want for wrapping indices.
`7 / 2` is evaluated first, as `int`, and has already lost the half.
One `double` operand makes the division exact.
The true value is 2 147 488 281, past `Integer.MAX_VALUE`; it wraps silently.
The cast applies to the left operand *before* multiplying.
The cast applies *after* an `int` multiply that already overflowed.
traces.takeaway: Every wrong row in a first submission is one of three things: integer division that happened earlier than you thought, a negative remainder, or an `int` that overflowed before it was widened. The fix is always to decide the type *before* the operation.

costs.note: Fine up to ~10⁵ tokens; BufferedReader is the upgrade beyond that.
Cost does not depend on the size of the numbers here.

pitfalls.symptom: `InputMismatchException` on the first read
pitfalls.cause: `nextInt()` hit a token that is not an integer — often because the input starts with a line of text, or a previous `nextLine()` consumed it.
pitfalls.fix: Match the read calls to the input format line by line before running.

pitfalls.symptom: The line you read back is empty
pitfalls.cause: `nextInt()` leaves the newline behind; the next `nextLine()` returns that empty remainder rather than the following line.
pitfalls.fix: Call `sc.nextLine()` once to discard the remainder before reading real text.

pitfalls.symptom: Correct on small cases, wrong on the big one
pitfalls.cause: `int` overflow. The wrong answer is often negative or wildly small.
pitfalls.fix: Do the arithmetic in `long`, casting before the multiply: `(long) a * b`.

pitfalls.symptom: Off by one on a division
pitfalls.cause: Integer division truncates toward zero rather than rounding.
pitfalls.fix: For a ceiling of `a / b` with positive values, write `(a + b - 1) / b`.

checks.q: What does `7 / 2` evaluate to in Java, and what about `-7 / 2`?
checks.a: `3` and `-3`. Integer division truncates **toward zero**, so the negative case rounds up rather than down.

checks.q: `int a = 100000, b = 100000; long c = a * b;` — what is `c`?
checks.a: `1410065408`, not 10¹⁰. The multiply happens in `int` and overflows *before* the widening to `long`. Write `(long) a * b`.

checks.q: Why does `sc.nextLine()` sometimes return an empty string?
checks.a: Because `nextInt()` stops at the end of the number and leaves the newline in the buffer. The next `nextLine()` consumes that remainder.

checks.q: The expected output is `Hello, World!` and you print `hello, world!`. Pass or fail?
checks.a: Fail. The judge normalises trailing whitespace only — the text itself is compared exactly, capitalisation included.

bigo.why: One read per number. Reading the input is part of the cost — no program that must look at n numbers can be faster than O(n), which is why that is the floor for most problems.

bigo.code:
long total = (long) n * (n + 1) / 2;
System.out.println(total);
bigo.why: Arithmetic on fixed-width numbers costs the same whether `n` is 3 or 2 billion. A formula replacing a loop is the purest complexity win there is — and the `(long)` cast is what keeps it correct, not what makes it fast.
Strings are immutable, so every `+=` copies everything built so far: 1 + 2 + … + n characters. It looks like one loop and is quadratic in the output size. Build output with a `StringBuilder`.

`append` is amortised O(1): the buffer doubles when full, so the total copying is bounded by twice the final length. Same output as the `+=` loop, one complexity class cheaper — the difference is invisible at n = 100 and a timeout at n = 10⁵.
Two independent sizes stay two variables. Calling this O(n²) is only right when the grid is square — and it is *linear* in the input, because the input is r·c numbers.

units.interview:
Nobody asks "add two numbers" in an interview — but every interview starts with
you restating the input format, and roughly a third of failed phone screens are
really *"I never confirmed what the input looked like"*. The habit this unit
builds is the one that matters: read the format out loud, name the types, and
say where overflow could happen, before writing a line.

units.next_up:
You can read, compute and print. The next unit asks the program to make a
decision instead of always doing the same thing.

units.title: Branching & Conditions
units.tagline: Pick an answer instead of computing one.
units.why:
A formula gives the same shape of answer every time. The moment a problem says
*"if … otherwise …"*, *"the larger of"*, or *"is it …?"*, the program has to
choose a branch. Getting that right is mostly about one thing people skip:
enumerating the cases and checking they are **exhaustive and non-overlapping**.

Every later unit leans on this. A binary search is three cases; a DP transition
is a `max` over cases; a graph traversal is "visited or not". Branching is
never *the* algorithm — it is the joint that every algorithm is built from.
units.model:
### Cases, not conditions

Write the cases down before the code. Three questions:

1. **Are they exhaustive?** Does every possible input match one?
2. **Do they overlap?** If two can be true at once, the *first* one wins — so
   order matters. `n % 15 == 0` must be tested before `n % 3 == 0`.
3. **Where are the boundaries?** The bug is almost always at `==`, at zero, or
   at a negative value.

### The three forms

```java
if (cond) { ... } else { ... }          // two cases
if (a) { } else if (b) { } else { }     // ordered chain, first match wins
cond ? x : y                            // an expression, when both sides are values
```

A `boolean` is already a value — `return n % 2 == 0;` is better than
`if (n % 2 == 0) return true; else return false;`, and the difference is not
style: the second form is where a stray `=` hides.

### Comparison traps

- `&&` and `||` **short-circuit**: the right side is skipped when the left
  settles it. That is what makes `i < n && a[i] == x` safe.
- For `String`, `==` compares *references*. Always `a.equals(b)`.
- Chaining does not work: `a < b < c` does not compile. Write `a < b && b < c`.

signals.why: Return the comparison itself; no `if` is needed.
Built-ins say what you mean and cannot be mistyped.
The word is the statement telling you the chain must be exhaustive.
An ordered chain takes the first match, so the combined case goes first.

skeletons.name: Boolean answer
skeletons.when: “Is n even?”, “is it a leap year?”, “does it satisfy …?”
skeletons.note: Never `if (x) return true; else return false;` — return `x`.

skeletons.name: Ordered case chain
skeletons.when: Several rules where more than one can apply.
skeletons.note: Most specific first. Reordering these two lines is the classic FizzBuzz bug.

skeletons.name: Max of three
skeletons.when: Extending a two-way comparison without nesting `if`s.
skeletons.code: int best = Math.max(a, Math.max(b, c));
skeletons.note: Nesting `Math.max` scales; nesting `if`/`else` past three cases does not.

traces.title: Order matters in an else-if chain: FizzBuzz, two ways
traces.intro: Both chains test the same three conditions. The left one checks `% 15` first; the right one checks it last. The chain stops at the first true branch.
traces.takeaway: The chains agree on every row except the ones divisible by 15, where the `% 3` branch fires first and the `% 15` branch is unreachable. When conditions overlap, the most specific one goes first — and a branch that can never run is a bug even if it compiles.

costs.note: Constant in practice — but a condition that scans an array is not O(1).

pitfalls.symptom: The condition is always true
pitfalls.cause: `=` typed instead of `==`. In Java this only compiles for `boolean`, which is exactly where it does the most damage.
pitfalls.fix: Put the constant on the left (`if (0 == n)`) if you keep making this typo.

pitfalls.symptom: Strings that look equal compare as different
pitfalls.cause: `==` on `String` compares object identity, not characters.
pitfalls.fix: `a.equals(b)`, or `a.equalsIgnoreCase(b)` when case should not matter.

pitfalls.symptom: Right answer for positives, wrong for 0 or negatives
pitfalls.cause: The case list was written with only positive input in mind.
pitfalls.fix: Test the boundary explicitly: `0`, `-1`, and the constraint's extremes.

pitfalls.symptom: FizzBuzz prints `Fizz` where `FizzBuzz` was expected
pitfalls.cause: The `% 3` branch is tested before the `% 15` branch and wins first.
pitfalls.fix: Order overlapping cases most-specific first.

checks.q: Why is `if (i < n && a[i] == x)` safe when `i` may equal `n`?
checks.a: `&&` short-circuits: when `i < n` is false the right side is never evaluated, so the out-of-bounds read never happens. Swapping the order crashes.

checks.q: What is wrong with `if (s == "yes")`?
checks.a: It compares references, not text. It may even appear to work for literals because of interning, which makes the bug worse. Use `s.equals("yes")`.

checks.q: Rewrite `if (n % 2 == 0) return true; else return false;`
checks.a: `return n % 2 == 0;` — the comparison already produces the boolean.

bigo.why: The number of comparisons is fixed by the code, not by the input. A chain of ten `else if`s is still O(1); a chain whose length depends on the data would not be.
The inner loop is inside a branch taken exactly once, so it adds n, not n·n. Price how often a branch runs, not whether it contains a loop.
Complexity is the worst case unless you say otherwise, and the worst case is every element even. "It only runs for half of them" is a factor of ½, which does not change the class.
The early return makes the *best* case O(1) — target at index 0 — but the question without a qualifier is the worst case: the target absent, every element checked.
Sorting is O(n log n) in the *length of the array*, and the length is 3. Sorting a fixed-size array is a constant amount of work — often the clearest way to avoid a tangle of comparisons.

units.interview:
Interviewers read your case analysis as a proxy for your rigour. Saying *"three
cases: empty, single element, and the general one"* before you type buys more
credit than any clever line you write afterwards — and it is the same habit that
catches the empty-array bug in the array unit.

notes.triangle-type: Order the branches from most specific to least; the impossible case overrides all.
notes.quadrant-of-point: Boundary cases first, so the general branches can assume non-zero coordinates.

units.next_up:
You can choose. The next unit repeats — and repetition is where arithmetic on
the *digits* of a number becomes possible.

units.title: Loops & Digit Arithmetic
units.tagline: Repeat until something runs out — including a number's digits.
units.why:
A loop is the first idea in this curriculum whose *cost depends on the input*,
which makes it the first place Big-O means anything at all. It is also where a
second, sneakier skill appears: taking a number apart with `% 10` and `/ 10`,
without ever converting it to a string.

That digit loop shows up far past this stage — in palindromic numbers, in
digital roots, in the base conversion that hides inside bit manipulation. It is
worth being fluent in it now, while the problems are small.
units.model:
### The two loop shapes

```java
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { ... }   // a known number of steps
while (n > 0) { ... }                 // until a condition breaks
```

Use `for` when you can say the trip count in advance, and `while` when the body
is what changes the condition. Every `while` needs an answer to *"what makes
this stop?"* — if you cannot say it in a sentence, you have written an infinite
loop.

### Taking a number apart

```java
while (n > 0) {
    int d = n % 10;   // the last digit
    n /= 10;          // drop it
}
```

Three facts make this work, and each one is a bug when forgotten:

- It reads digits **right to left**. If order matters, build the answer in
  reverse or push the digits somewhere.
- It runs **⌊log₁₀ n⌋ + 1 times** — about 10 iterations for an `int`. Digit
  loops are effectively free; that is why they beat string conversion.
- It **never runs for `n == 0`**. A zero-digit-count answer for the input `0` is
  the single most common wrong answer in this unit.

### Accumulators

Almost every loop here carries a value across iterations: a `sum`, a `count`, a
`best`, a `reversed`. Name it for what it holds, initialise it where the empty
case is correct (`sum = 0`, `count = 0`, `product = 1`), and update it exactly
once per iteration.

signals.when: “sum / count / product of the first n …”
signals.why: Trip count known up front.

signals.when: “digits of n”, “sum of digits”, “reverse the number”
signals.why: Cheap, exact, and avoids string conversion entirely.
The body changes the value the condition tests.
Reversing digits is the same `% 10` loop with an accumulator.

skeletons.name: Accumulate over a range
skeletons.when: Sums, counts, factorials — anything with a known trip count.
skeletons.note: `long` because a sum of n terms grows far faster than any single term.

skeletons.name: Walk the digits
skeletons.when: Digit sums, digit counts, digital roots, digit filters.
skeletons.note: Handle `0` outside the loop, and `Math.abs` before it if input may be negative.

skeletons.name: Reverse a number
skeletons.when: Palindromic numbers, reversed integers.
skeletons.note: `long` for `rev`: reversing a valid `int` can overflow an `int`.

traces.title: Reversing the digits of 4705
traces.intro: `n % 10` peels off the last digit and `n / 10` drops it. `rev * 10 + d` appends that digit to the right of `rev`.
traces.takeaway: Four iterations for four digits — the loop runs once per digit, which is why this is O(log n). The leading `5` of 4705 becomes the trailing digit of 5074, and the internal `0` survives because `rev * 10` shifts it into place. A *trailing* zero would vanish: reversing 4700 gives 74.

costs.note: ≤ 10 iterations for an `int` — cheaper than any string conversion.
Fine at n ≤ 3,000; the wall the whole next stage exists to avoid.

pitfalls.symptom: The answer is 0 when the input is 0
pitfalls.cause: `while (n > 0)` never executes, so the accumulator keeps its initial value.
pitfalls.fix: Treat `n == 0` as an explicit case before the loop.

pitfalls.symptom: The program hangs
pitfalls.cause: A `while` whose body does not move it toward the stopping condition — a forgotten `n /= 10`, or dividing by a value that can be 1.
pitfalls.fix: State the stopping condition in a sentence; if you cannot, the loop is wrong.

pitfalls.symptom: Reversing a large number gives a negative result
pitfalls.cause: The reversed value left `int` range mid-loop.
pitfalls.fix: Accumulate in `long` and compare afterwards.

pitfalls.symptom: Off by one in the last iteration
pitfalls.cause: `<` versus `<=`, or starting at 1 where the problem counts from 0.
pitfalls.fix: Say what the *first* and *last* values of `i` should be, then write the header.

checks.q: How many times does `while (n > 0) { n /= 10; }` run for n = 4,096?
checks.a: Four — once per digit. Generally ⌊log₁₀ n⌋ + 1, which is at most 10 for an `int`.

checks.q: Why initialise a product accumulator to 1 and a sum accumulator to 0?
checks.a: They are the identity elements: combining with them changes nothing, so the empty case comes out right without a special branch.

checks.q: Why compute a digit sum with `% 10` instead of `String.valueOf(n)`?
checks.a: It avoids allocating a string and parsing characters, it cannot pick up a minus sign by accident, and it is the same loop you will reuse for base-2.

checks.q: What is `-7 % 3` in Java, and why does it matter here?
checks.a: `-1` — the remainder keeps the sign of the left operand. A digit loop on a negative number therefore produces negative digits unless you `Math.abs` first.

bigo.why: One iteration per candidate divisor up to the value n. Divisors come in pairs `(d, n/d)`, so stopping at `d * d <= n` and counting both halves makes it O(√n) — that trick belongs to the number-theory unit.

bigo.code:
int steps = 0;
for (long p = 1; p <= n; p *= 2) steps++;
bigo.why: `p` doubles, so it passes n after ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 steps. Whenever the loop variable is *multiplied* or *divided*, look for a log.

bigo.code:
int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i * i <= n; i++) count++;
bigo.why: The loop stops once i² exceeds n, i.e. once i passes √n. The condition, not the increment, decides how long a loop runs.
The inner loop runs ten times whatever n is, so it is a constant factor. Nested loops multiply their *counts*, and one of these counts is 10.
Each i has about log₁₀ i digits, and summing log i over 1…n gives Θ(n log n). In practice the inner loop runs at most 10 times for an `int`, which is why this is fast — but the growth is n log n.

units.interview:
"What is the complexity?" gets asked about the code you just wrote, and a digit
loop is the first place the honest answer is not O(n). Saying *O(log n) in the
value of n, which is at most 10 iterations here* is a small thing that signals
you distinguish the size of the input from the size of the number in it.

units.title: Arrays: The First Pass
units.tagline: One scan, one accumulator, and the index bugs that come free with them.
units.why:
An array is the first data structure, and *single-pass scanning* is the first
algorithm. Roughly a third of every problem bank — including a surprising
number of the Mediums — is a single pass with a cleverer accumulator, so this
unit is not a warm-up you outgrow: it is the shape you will keep returning to.

It is also where the two eternal array bugs first appear: reading `a[n]`, and
seeding a maximum with `0` when the data can be negative.
units.model:
### What an array actually is

A single fixed-length block of slots, indexed `0 … a.length - 1`. The length is
decided at creation and never changes. `a[a.length]` is always out of bounds —
the `<` in `i < a.length` is not a style choice.

### The single-pass template

```java
int best = a[0];                  // seed from the data, never from 0
for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
    if (a[i] > best) best = a[i];
}
```

Three decisions, and each one is a bug in waiting:

1. **What does the accumulator hold?** Say it in words: *"the largest value seen
   so far"*. If you cannot, you do not yet have the algorithm.
2. **What is it seeded with?** Seed from the data (`a[0]`) or from a value the
   data cannot beat (`Integer.MIN_VALUE`). `0` is wrong the moment values can be
   negative, and it is wrong silently.
3. **Does the empty array make sense?** `a[0]` on an empty array throws. If the
   constraints permit `n = 0`, decide the answer before the loop.

### When one accumulator is not enough

*Second largest* needs two, and updating them in the right order is the whole
problem: when a new champion arrives, the old champion becomes the runner-up.
Trying to do it with one variable and a second pass is where most wrong answers
come from.

### Counting

"How many elements satisfy P?" is the same template with `count++` in the body.
If P depends on something global — an average, a maximum — you need **two
passes**: compute the global first, then count. Two passes is still O(n); it is
not something to avoid.

signals.when: “sum / count / max / min of the array”
signals.why: Nothing needs to be stored; the running value is the answer.
Pass 1 computes the average, pass 2 counts against it.
A property of adjacent pairs never needs more than `a[i-1]` and `a[i]`.
Update the runner-up in the same branch that replaces the champion.

signals.reach_for: A current-run counter plus a best-so-far
signals.why: Reset the current counter the moment the run breaks.

rows: new minimum — a better day to buy
new minimum — a better day to buy
traces.takeaway: The answer is 5 — buy at 1, sell at 6 — found without comparing any pair of days. Checking every pair is O(n²); carrying the minimum is O(n), because the only earlier day that matters is the cheapest one.

costs.note: The floor: you must at least look at every element.
Still linear. Do not contort the code to avoid it.
Acceptable to about n = 3,000; the reason the next stage exists.
Indexing is arithmetic, not a search.

pitfalls.symptom: `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`
pitfalls.cause: `i <= a.length` in the loop header, or comparing `a[i]` with `a[i + 1]` on the last iteration.
pitfalls.fix: When the body touches `a[i + 1]`, the header must stop at `a.length - 1`.

pitfalls.symptom: The maximum comes out as 0 on all-negative input
pitfalls.cause: `best` was seeded with `0`, which no negative value can beat.
pitfalls.fix: Seed from `a[0]` (and start the loop at 1) or from `Integer.MIN_VALUE`.

pitfalls.symptom: A sum is wrong only on the largest test
pitfalls.cause: The sum overflowed `int` even though every element fits.
pitfalls.fix: Accumulate sums in `long`.

pitfalls.symptom: `second == best` when the array has duplicates
pitfalls.cause: The runner-up branch accepted a value equal to the champion.
pitfalls.fix: Decide what the problem means by *second largest* for `[5, 5, 3]`, then make the strictness of the comparison match.

pitfalls.symptom: Crash on an empty array
pitfalls.cause: `a[0]` was read to seed an accumulator without checking `n > 0`.
pitfalls.fix: Decide the empty-array answer explicitly when the constraints allow `n = 0`.

checks.q: Why seed a maximum with `a[0]` rather than `0`?
checks.a: Because `0` is a value the data might never exceed. On `[-5, -2, -9]` the `0` seed reports `0`, which is not in the array at all.

checks.q: Is a two-pass solution worse than a one-pass one?
checks.a: Not asymptotically — both are O(n). Prefer whichever is clearer; only collapse passes when a measurement or a constraint asks for it.

checks.q: In the longest-run template, why does `run` reset to 0 rather than 1?
checks.a: Because the element that broke the run is not part of any run. Resetting to 1 would count the breaking element itself.

checks.q: What is the cost of `a[i]` compared with searching for a value in `a`?
checks.a: `a[i]` is O(1) address arithmetic; searching is O(n). Confusing the two is the root of most accidental O(n²) code.

bigo.why: The copy is a hidden O(n) and the swap loop is n/2 — O(n) + O(n) is O(n). Library calls that touch every element cost what a loop over every element costs.
Inserting at the front shifts everything already stored: 0 + 1 + … + (n−1) moves. Arrays are cheap at the end and expensive at the front — build it reversed, or use an `ArrayDeque`.
Each entry reuses the one before it, so a running maximum is one pass. This is the smallest possible dynamic-programming idea, and it is worth recognising as one.
Same output as the running maximum, recomputed from scratch at every i: 0 + 1 + … + (n−1) comparisons. When the answer at i only extends the answer at i−1, carry it instead of rebuilding it.
`Arrays.fill` is a loop over n. Resetting a whole array per query multiplies the query count by the array size — undo only the entries you set, or stamp each entry with the query number instead.

units.interview:
Every array interview opens with the same three questions, and asking them
yourself scores the points: *Can it be empty? Can values be negative? How large
can the sum get?* Each maps directly onto a pitfall above — and each is a real
bug in the code most candidates write when they skip them.

rungs.title: Warm up
rungs.purpose: One pass, one accumulator.

notes.array-maximum: Try it once with a `0` seed on all-negative input, so the bug is one you have actually seen.

rungs.title: Core
rungs.purpose: Accumulators that carry a little more state.

notes.max-consecutive-ones: Extend-or-reset. This exact pair of lines returns as Kadane's algorithm.

rungs.title: Variations
rungs.purpose: Properties of neighbours, and of the array as a whole.

notes.is-sorted: The first problem where the loop must stop at `a.length - 1`, because the body reads `a[i + 1]`.
notes.is-permutation-1n: A seen-array indexed by value — the first hint of the hashing idea two units away.
notes.leaders-in-array: From the right, 'bigger than everything after it' needs one number: the maximum so far.
notes.plus-one-digits: The schoolbook carry on a digit array. Only all-9s makes the number longer.
notes.set-mismatch: Values in 1..n are indices in disguise: a count array finds both answers in one scan.

rungs.title: Extra practice
rungs.purpose: More single passes — optional, counted only once started.

notes.even-digit-numbers: A tiny inner loop per element keeps the scan effectively linear.
notes.check-rotated-sorted: Describe every rotation instead of searching for one: at most one cyclic drop.
notes.max-ascending-subarray-sum: A running sum that resets when the order breaks.
notes.can-place-flowers: Plant at the earliest valid plot; edges count as empty neighbours.
notes.third-maximum: Three slots of distinct maxima, with a sentinel outside the int range.

units.next_up:
You can scan. The next stage asks the question that turns scanning into
engineering: *how expensive is this, and can it be cheaper?*

stages.title: Cost & Core Patterns
stages.tagline: Stop re-reading what you have already seen.
stages.goal:
Every technique in this stage removes a nested loop, and each removes it a
different way:

| Pattern | The work it reuses |
| --- | --- |
| **Cost** | Nothing — it is how you decide *which* of the others you can afford |
| **Hashing** | *“Have I seen this value?”* — answered in O(1) instead of a scan |
| **Two pointers** | Sorted order, so neither pointer ever needs to go back |
| **Sliding window** | The previous window's answer, adjusted at both ends |
| **Prefix sums** | Every range sum, precomputed once |
| **Strings** | All four of the above, with a `char` costume and a copying trap |

Learn to recognise which one a prompt is asking for and the Medium tier stops
looking like a different sport from the Easy tier. That recognition is the
skill; the code is four short templates you will have memorised by the end of
the stage.

**The hard part is not the templates, it is telling them apart.** Six units that
all take an array and return a number, and prompts that differ by one word:
*longest* versus *shortest*, *at most k* versus *exactly k*, *subarray* versus
*subsequence*. The routing table below is that distinction written down — read
it before the units, and again after.

router.when: “does this value appear / appear twice / have a partner”
router.why: Membership and counting. Anything answerable by a lookup rather than a scan.
router.not_when: “does this *range* sum to …” is prefix sums + a map, not a plain set.

router.when: “find a pair that sums to / differs by a target”
router.why: One lookup for the complement. O(n) time, O(n) space, and the original indices survive.
router.not_when: If the array is **sorted**, or O(1) space is demanded, it is two pointers instead.

router.when: The input is **sorted**, and the answer is a pair or a triple
router.why: Sorted order lets one comparison retire a whole row of the pair table. O(1) space.
router.not_when: Unsorted input where the answer is the original indices — sorting destroys them, so hash it.

router.when: “in place”, “without extra space”, “remove / partition / reverse”
router.why: A read pointer and a write pointer, moving the same way. Nothing is allocated.

router.when: “contiguous subarray / substring”, **longest** or **shortest**
router.why: One window whose left edge never rewinds. The word *contiguous* is the signal.
router.not_when: **Subsequence** is not contiguous — that is dynamic programming, four stages away.

router.when: “at most k …” in a contiguous run
router.why: Validity survives shrinking, which is exactly what the window's invariant needs.
router.not_when: “**exactly** k” is not a window: run *at most k* twice and subtract.

router.when: “every window of size k”
router.why: Fixed width, so there is no shrink loop — add the entrant, remove the leaver.
router.not_when: If the summary is a max or min rather than a sum, it needs a monotonic deque (queues unit).

router.when: “how many subarrays sum to k”, with negatives allowed
router.why: Every subarray is a *pair of prefixes*, so a map counts them without enumerating them. Negatives are fine.
router.not_when: All-positive values and a *longest/shortest* question is a window, which is O(1) space.

router.when: “many range queries on an array that never changes”
router.why: Pay O(n) once, answer each query by one subtraction.
router.not_when: If the array **is** updated between queries, this unit cannot help — that is a Fenwick tree, in the optional stage.

router.when: “add v to every index in [l, r]”, repeated
router.why: A difference array: mark the two edges, prefix-sum once at the end.

router.when: “maximum simultaneous …”, overlapping intervals
router.why: A ±1 sweep over the endpoints. The array is a timeline.
router.not_when: Merging or scheduling the intervals themselves is the `intervals` unit, next stage.

router.when: Anagrams, palindromes, character counts, common prefixes
router.why: Array techniques with a `char` costume — plus the Java-specific traps around copying.

router.when: “will this pass at n = …”, “what is the complexity”
router.why: Read the constraint first: it tells you which of the other five shapes is affordable before you write anything.

units.title: Cost: Big-O in Practice
units.tagline: Count the work before you write it, and know when n² is fine.
units.why:
Every problem you have solved so far was small enough that nothing you wrote
could be too slow. That ends here. From this unit on, the interesting question
is never *"does it work?"* but *"does it work at n = 200,000?"* — and the answer
has to be decidable **before** you type, because a wrong choice of approach is
not something you can patch afterwards.

Big-O gets taught as a maths topic. It is really a *budgeting* topic: you are
given a constraint, you have roughly 10⁸ simple operations to spend, and the
constraint tells you which shapes of solution fit.
units.model:
### Read the constraint, pick the shape

A rough but reliable table. Take the largest `n` in the constraints and read
off what you can afford:

| n up to | Budget allows | Typical approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10–12 | O(n!) | Permutations, brute force |
| 20–25 | O(2ⁿ) | Subsets, bitmask DP |
| 500 | O(n³) | Triple loop, Floyd–Warshall |
| 5,000 | O(n²) | Every pair, 2-D DP |
| 10⁵–10⁶ | O(n log n) | Sort, heap, binary search |
| 10⁶–10⁷ | O(n) | One pass, hashing, two pointers |
| 10⁹+ | O(log n) or O(1) | Binary search on the answer, a formula |

Read it backwards too, and it becomes a *hint*: a constraint of `n ≤ 20` is the
setter telling you an exponential search is intended. A constraint of `n ≤ 10⁵`
is them telling you O(n²) will time out.

### Counting the work

Big-O keeps the fastest-growing term and drops constants, because at large n
nothing else matters:

- **Sequential** code adds: O(n) then O(n) is O(n). Two passes are still linear.
- **Nested** code multiplies: a loop inside a loop over the same data is O(n²).
- **Halving** is logarithmic: each step throws away half the remaining input, so
  it finishes in about log₂ n steps — 20 for a million, 30 for a billion.
- **A call inside a loop counts.** `list.contains(x)` inside a `for` is O(n²),
  and it is the most common accidental quadratic there is, because the nesting
  is hidden behind a method name.

### Amortized cost: price the loop, not the step

Counting by nesting has a blind spot, and it is the one that makes people
"optimise" code that was already linear:

```java
Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    while (!st.isEmpty() && a[st.peek()] < a[i]) st.pop();   // a loop, inside a loop
    st.push(i);
}
```

Two nested loops, so O(n²)? No — **O(n)**. The inner `while` can only pop what
some earlier iteration pushed, and each index is pushed once. The right question
is not *"how many steps can one iteration take?"* (n, in the worst case) but
*"how many steps can the whole loop take?"* (2n: one push and one pop per index).
Divide by n and each iteration costs **O(1) amortized**.

That is the whole idea:

> **Amortized cost = total work over a sequence of operations ÷ the number of
> operations.** It is a worst case, not an average — no lucky input is assumed.

The accounting argument is always the same shape: find a quantity that each
operation pays into, and show that every expensive step spends what an earlier
cheap step deposited. For the stack, the deposit is the push.

You have already relied on this without naming it:

| Where | Why one step looks expensive | Why the sequence is cheap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ArrayList.add` | Occasionally copies the whole array | Doubling: n adds copy 1 + 2 + 4 + … < 2n elements, so **O(1) amortized** |
| Two pointers | The inner pointer can jump far | Neither pointer ever moves backwards — 2n moves total |
| Sliding window | One shrink can empty the window | Every element enters and leaves once |
| Monotonic stack | One iteration can pop everything | Each index is pushed once and popped once |
| Union-find | One `find` can walk a long chain | Path compression flattens it; the sequence is near-constant per call |

### Amortized is not average, and not per-call

Three different claims, often muddled:

- **Worst case per call** — `ArrayList.add` is O(n) on the call that resizes.
  True, and it is what a latency-sensitive system cares about.
- **Amortized** — n calls cost O(n) *total*, guaranteed, on every input.
- **Average case** — assumes a distribution over inputs (quickselect's O(n) is
  this kind, and an adversary can break it; amortized cannot be broken).

Say "amortized O(1)" when you mean the sequence, and be ready for the follow-up:
*"is there a single call that is slow?"* For a doubling array, yes — and that is
why a real-time system pre-sizes it.

### Space

Same counting, applied to memory you allocate. An extra array is O(n); a fixed
26-slot counter is O(1). Recursion costs stack depth even when it allocates
nothing — a recursion n deep is O(n) space.

### When O(n²) is the right answer

When n is small, when the quadratic version is obviously correct and the linear
one is delicate, or when you need a baseline to test the fast one against.
"Optimal" is defined by the constraints, not by pride.

signals.why: The constraint is a hint that nothing polynomial is expected.
Do the simple thing; a clever linear solution is wasted effort.
Quadratic will time out. Sort, hash or two-pointer it.

signals.when: Values up to 10⁹ but few of them
signals.why: Cost tracks the count of items, not the size of the numbers.
The hidden inner scan makes an innocent-looking loop quadratic.

signals.when: An inner `while` that can only undo what an outer step did
signals.reach_for: Count the whole loop, not one iteration
signals.why: Amortized O(1): each item is added once, so it can be removed once.

skeletons.name: The accidental quadratic
skeletons.when: Recognise this shape — it is the single most common performance bug.
skeletons.note: `Set.add` returning `false` is the idiomatic “I have seen this before”.

skeletons.name: Counting sort / frequency array
skeletons.when: When the values are small integers or letters, counting beats sorting.
skeletons.code:
int[] freq = new int[26];               // O(1) space — 26 is a constant
for (char c : s.toCharArray()) freq[c - 'a']++;
skeletons.note: O(n) time, O(1) space. The alphabet is a constant, however big it feels.

skeletons.name: The amortized argument, written out
skeletons.when: Whenever an inner loop can only undo work an outer step did.
skeletons.note: Name the deposit (`push`) and the withdrawal (`pop`), then bound the deposits. That sentence is the proof, and it is what an interviewer wants to hear.

traces.title: How the classes grow: steps for each input size
traces.intro: Rough operation counts, with a budget of about 10⁸ simple steps per second as the yardstick. Read down a column to see where each class stops being feasible.
traces.takeaway: At n = 20, 2ⁿ is a million — fine. At n = 10⁵, n² is 10¹⁰ — a hundred seconds — while n log n is under 2·10⁶. That is why constraints are a hint: n ≤ 20 invites exponential search, n ≤ 10⁵ demands n log n or better, and n ≤ 10⁶ wants linear.

traces.title: Why `ArrayList.add` is O(1) amortized
traces.intro: An array that doubles when full. Column 3 is what *this* call costs; column 5 is the total work so far divided by the number of calls — the amortized cost.
traces.takeaway: The expensive calls never go away — add 17 would copy 16 elements — but they get rarer at exactly the rate they get costlier, so the last column stays under 3 forever. The copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 …, and 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n < 2n. Growing by a fixed +1 instead would make column 5 climb without limit: that is the same loop, genuinely O(n²).

costs.note: Binary search, heap push/pop, tree descent.
A pass. The floor for anything that must read all input.
Sorting. The usual cost of imposing order.
Every pair. Check the constraint first.
Every subset. Only viable because n is tiny.
`ArrayList.add`, a monotonic stack step. One call may still be O(n).

pitfalls.symptom: “Time limit exceeded” on the large test only
pitfalls.cause: The approach is a tier too slow — usually a hidden inner scan.
pitfalls.fix: Count the loops, including the ones inside library calls, then re-read the constraint.

pitfalls.symptom: Optimising code that was never the bottleneck
pitfalls.cause: Constant-factor tinkering inside an O(n²) algorithm.
pitfalls.fix: Change the shape, not the constant. O(n log n) beats a tuned O(n²) at any interesting n.

pitfalls.symptom: `String` concatenation in a loop is mysteriously slow
pitfalls.cause: `s += x` allocates a whole new string each time, making the loop O(n²) in total characters.
pitfalls.fix: Accumulate with `StringBuilder` and call `toString()` once.

pitfalls.symptom: Claiming O(n) for something that sorts
pitfalls.cause: Sorting is O(n log n); a single call can dominate everything around it.
pitfalls.fix: State the complexity of every library call you make, not just your loops.

pitfalls.symptom: Calling a monotonic-stack or sliding-window loop O(n²)
pitfalls.cause: The inner `while` was counted as n, when it can only remove what an outer step added.
pitfalls.fix: Bound the *total* removals over the whole loop, not the removals in one iteration. n additions allow at most n removals — O(n) overall.

pitfalls.symptom: Saying “amortized” when the claim is really “average case”
pitfalls.cause: Both mean “usually fast”, but only one of them survives an adversary.
pitfalls.fix: Amortized is a guarantee over a sequence on *every* input; average case assumes a distribution. Quickselect is average O(n); `ArrayList.add` is amortized O(1).

checks.q: A problem says `1 ≤ n ≤ 200000`. Is an O(n²) solution acceptable?
checks.a: No — that is 4×10¹⁰ operations. The constraint is telling you to find an O(n log n) or O(n) approach.

checks.q: Why is `for (x : a) if (list.contains(x))` quadratic?
checks.a: `contains` on a list is itself a linear scan, so the loop nests one O(n) operation inside another. A `HashSet` makes the inner step O(1).

checks.q: Are two sequential O(n) passes worse than one?
checks.a: Not in Big-O — O(n) + O(n) = O(n). Only the constant factor differs, and clarity usually wins that trade.

checks.q: What is the space complexity of a recursion that goes n levels deep and allocates nothing?
checks.a: O(n) — every pending call keeps a frame on the stack. Deep recursion is a memory cost even when it looks free.

checks.q: `n ≤ 22` and the problem asks for every possible selection. What does that hint?
checks.a: That 2ⁿ ≈ 4 million is the intended cost — enumerate the subsets, and do not hunt for a polynomial trick that probably does not exist.

checks.q: A loop over n items has an inner `while` that can pop the whole stack. Why is it O(n) and not O(n²)?
checks.a: Because the pops are paid for by the pushes. Each index is pushed once, so across the entire loop there are at most n pops — no single iteration's worst case can happen n times. Total work 2n, i.e. O(1) amortized per iteration.

checks.q: What is the difference between amortized O(1) and average-case O(1)?
checks.a: Amortized is a guarantee about a *sequence* of operations that holds on every input; average case assumes a distribution over inputs and can be defeated by an adversary. `ArrayList.add` is amortized O(1); a hash lookup is average O(1).

checks.q: Is `ArrayList.add` ever slow?
checks.a: Yes — the call that triggers a resize copies every element, so that one call is O(n). Amortized O(1) says n adds cost O(n) in total; it does not promise any individual call is cheap. Pre-size the list if that matters.

bigo.code:
long sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i];
bigo.why: One pass, one constant-time body. The floor for any problem that has to look at every element.
n(n−1)/2 pairs. Starting the inner loop at `i + 1` halves the work and changes nothing asymptotically — a constant factor is not a complexity.

One iteration per *digit*, so ⌊log₁₀ n⌋ + 1 — at most 10 for an `int`. Note that this is log in the **value** of n, not in the size of a collection. Calling it O(1) because it never exceeds 10 is defensible in conversation and wrong on paper; say which you mean.

bigo.code:
Arrays.sort(a);
for (int x : a) if (set.contains(x)) hits++;
bigo.why: The sort dominates: O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n). The library call is where the cost is, which is exactly the habit this unit is for — price the calls, not just your own loops.

bigo.code:
for (int x : a)
    if (list.contains(x)) hits++;   // list is an ArrayList
bigo.why: `ArrayList.contains` is a linear scan, so an O(n) operation is nested inside an O(n) loop. This is the single most common accidental quadratic in real code, and it does not *look* nested. Swap the list for a `HashSet` and it is O(n).
The outer loop *multiplies*, so it runs log₂ n times; the inner one runs n. Nesting does not always mean squaring — read what the update does to the counter, not how many `for`s there are.

Two branches per call and depth n, so the call tree is exponential — about 1.6ⁿ to be precise, since it is the Fibonacci recurrence. Memoise it and the same function is O(n), which is the whole DP stage in one edit.
Linear time, and linear **space** — every pending call holds a stack frame. Deep recursion is a memory cost that looks free, and at n = 10⁶ it is a `StackOverflowError` rather than a slow answer.

bigo.answer: O(n²), which is linear in the input size
options: O(n²), which is linear in the input size
bigo.why: Both readings are right and the distinction matters. The grid holds n² cells, so reading all of them is O(n²) in n and O(size) in the actual input. Saying "quadratic" without saying *in what* is how a linear-time grid scan gets mistaken for something to optimise.

The range halves every iteration, so ⌈log₂ n⌉ iterations — 17 for 100,000 elements. The cost of *getting* the array sorted is not counted here, and forgetting to mention it is a common way to overstate a solution.

Two nested loops and still linear. The `while` can only pop indices some earlier iteration pushed, and each index is pushed exactly once — so at most n pops happen across the *whole* loop, not per iteration. That is amortized O(1) per step. Counting the inner loop as n here is the classic over-estimate.

bigo.code:
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) list.add(i);   // resizes by doubling when full
bigo.why: A resize copies everything, so *one* `add` can be O(n) — but the copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8 …, and 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n < 2n. Total O(n), i.e. O(1) amortized per add. Growing by a fixed +1 instead of doubling would make the same loop genuinely O(n²).

units.interview:
"What is the time and space complexity?" is asked in essentially every
interview, and the high-scoring version of the answer has three parts: the
complexity, *why* (the loops that produce it), and whether it is optimal
*given the constraints*. Volunteering the third part — "this is O(n log n)
because of the sort; O(n) is possible with counting since the values are
bounded" — is what separates a pass from a strong pass.

rungs.title: Core
rungs.purpose: Feel the difference between a quadratic and a linear solution on the same problem.

notes.second-largest: Solvable by sorting (O(n log n)) or by two accumulators (O(n)). Write both and compare.
notes.count-above-average: The two-pass solution people try to avoid. It is still O(n) — that is the lesson.
notes.count-equal-pairs: Every pair is O(n²); counting occurrences first makes it O(n). The gap here is the whole unit in one problem.
notes.sum-of-pair-products: The nested loops are right and 5·10⁹ steps at the limit. Read the inner loop as a sum you could carry instead.
notes.pairs-divisible-60: Only the remainder mod 60 matters — count the 60 kinds instead of checking pairs.
notes.sum-all-subarray-sums: O(n³), O(n²) or O(n) for the same total, depending on whether you count subarrays or contributions.

rungs.title: Stretch
rungs.purpose: Pay O(n log n) once to turn an O(n²) question into a linear pass.

notes.sum-abs-differences: The answer does not depend on the order of the array — so pick the order that deletes the absolute value.
notes.count-valid-triangles: Sorting turns three inequalities into one; then fix the longest side and count pairs.

rungs.title: Extra practice
rungs.purpose: More pair counting — optional, counted only once started.

notes.pairs-sum-less-than-target: Sort, then count a whole range of pairs in one step.
notes.number-of-good-pairs: Count each pair at its later index: billions of pairs in one pass.
notes.sum-subarray-ranges: Per-element contributions replace an O(n²) sweep over subarrays.
notes.sum-odd-length-subarrays: Swap the order of summation: count how many odd-length subarrays hold each element.

units.build_it:
### Price these three yourself, and then measure them

The goal is to stop trusting the table in this unit and start trusting an
experiment you ran.

**1. Write the timing harness.** A method that takes a `Runnable`, runs it once
to let the JIT warm up, then times it:

```java
static long millis(Runnable r) {
    r.run();                                  // warm-up — do NOT skip this
    long t = System.nanoTime();
    r.run();
    return (System.nanoTime() - t) / 1_000_000;
}
```

**2. Time three shapes** at n = 1,000 / 10,000 / 100,000 on random `int[]`s:

| Shape | What to write |
| --- | --- |
| O(n) | sum every element |
| O(n log n) | `Arrays.sort(a.clone())` |
| O(n²) | count pairs with `a[i] + a[j] == 0` |

**3. Read the ratios, not the times.** Ten times the input should cost:

- about **10×** for the linear pass;
- a little over **10×** for the sort (10 × log₁₀ of the ratio);
- about **100×** for the quadratic one.

The quadratic at n = 100,000 will take minutes. That is the point of the
exercise — stop it early and extrapolate from n = 10,000, which is itself the
skill this unit is about.

**4. Then find the surprise.** Time `list.contains` in a loop against
`set.contains` at n = 50,000. The ratio is not 2 or 10; it is in the thousands,
and the two versions look almost identical on the page.

**5. Finally, measure an amortized claim.** Append 10⁶ elements to an
`ArrayList`, then do the same to a list that grows by `+1` each time
(`Arrays.copyOf(a, a.length + 1)`). Doubling finishes instantly; +1 growth is
the same loop, genuinely O(n²), and watching it crawl is what makes "amortized
O(1)" stop being a phrase.
units.next_up:
`count-equal-pairs` became linear by *counting what it had seen*. Generalise
that and you have the most useful data structure in interview programming.

variants.name: Sequential passes
variants.change: Two loops one after another, not nested.
variants.when: A clean-up pass, then a compute pass.
variants.gotcha: Fusing them into one loop buys a constant factor and costs clarity. Do it when profiling says to, not by reflex.

variants.name: Nested over the same data
variants.change: The inner loop runs over the same n as the outer one.
variants.when: Every pair: comparisons, sums, collisions.
variants.gotcha: Starting the inner loop at `i + 1` halves the work and changes nothing asymptotically. A constant factor is not a complexity.

variants.name: Nested over different data
variants.change: The inner loop runs over a *second* collection of size m.
variants.when: Matching two lists, a grid of r × c.
variants.gotcha: Calling this "n²" is the most common imprecision in an interview answer. Say which n — and for an r × c grid, O(r·c) is *linear in the input*.

variants.name: Halving
variants.change: The counter is divided, not decremented.
variants.when: Binary search, tree descent, heap sift.
variants.gotcha: 20 steps at a million, 30 at a billion. Effectively constant, and worth saying so out loud when the constraint is 10⁹.

variants.name: Multiplying counter with an inner pass
variants.change: The outer counter multiplies; the inner one is linear.
variants.when: Doubling constructions: sparse tables, binary lifting, merge sort levels.
variants.gotcha: Two nested `for`s and *not* quadratic. Read what the update does to the counter, not how many loops there are.

variants.name: Digits or bits of a value
variants.change: The loop runs over `log₁₀ v` digits or `log₂ v` bits, not over n items.
variants.when: Digit sums, bit tricks, fast exponentiation.
variants.gotcha: This is log in the **value**, not in the size of a collection. Calling it O(1) because an `int` has at most 10 digits is defensible in conversation and wrong on paper — say which you mean.

variants.name: Hidden inner scan
variants.change: The inner loop is inside a method call, so the nesting is invisible.
variants.when: `list.contains`, `indexOf`, `String.substring`, `s += x`.
variants.gotcha: The single most common accidental quadratic in real code. Price every library call you make, not just the loops you typed.

variants.name: Inner loop that can only undo outer work
variants.change: The inner `while` removes only what an outer step added.
variants.when: Monotonic stacks, sliding windows, two pointers.
variants.gotcha: Counting the inner `while` as n here over-estimates by a whole tier. Bound the *total* removals, not one iteration's worst case.

variants.name: Branching recursion
variants.change: Each call makes two (or k) more.
variants.when: Naive Fibonacci, subset enumeration, unmemoised DP.
variants.gotcha: Add memoisation and the same function is O(n) or O(n²). That one edit is the entire DP stage, and it is worth recognising three stages early.

rewrites.title: The accidental quadratic
rewrites.edit: `ArrayList` → `HashSet`, and `contains` + `add` collapse into one `add`.
rewrites.why:
Nothing about the *logic* changed — the same elements are inserted and the same
question is asked. What changed is the cost of asking it: `ArrayList.contains`
walks the whole list, so an O(n) operation was sitting inside an O(n) loop and
the nesting was hidden behind a method name.

This is the shape to learn to see, because it does not look nested. Any time a
loop body calls something that searches, the loop is one tier slower than it
reads.

`Set.add` returning `false` for a duplicate is the idiomatic form — it does the
lookup and the insert in one hash of the key instead of two.

rewrites.title: Building a string in a loop
rewrites.edit: `String +=` → `StringBuilder.append`, with one `toString()` at the end.
rewrites.why:
Java strings are immutable, so `out += part` cannot extend `out` — it allocates
a new string and copies every character already there. Over n parts that is
1 + 2 + 3 + … characters copied, which is O(n²) in the total length.

`StringBuilder` keeps one mutable buffer and doubles it when full, so the n
appends cost O(n) **amortized** in total — the same doubling argument as
`ArrayList.add`.

The tell is any `+=` on a `String` inside a loop. On a few dozen parts it does
not matter; on 10⁵ it is the difference between instant and a timeout, and the
profiler will point at a line that looks innocent.

rewrites.title: Sorting when counting would do
rewrites.edit: `Arrays.sort` → a frequency array indexed by the value itself.
rewrites.why:
Sorting imposes a *total order* you never needed. The question is only "has this
value appeared before", and when the values are bounded — letters, digits,
`0 … 10⁵` — the value can be the index, which makes the lookup O(1) and the
whole pass O(n).

The condition is the bound. With values up to 10⁹ the frequency array is 4 GB
and this rewrite is worse than useless; that is when a `HashMap` takes its place
and you pay a constant factor instead of a log.

This is also the one rewrite here that is *not* always a win: it trades O(1)
extra space for O(V) where V is the value range. Say the trade out loud rather
than presenting it as free.

units.title: Hashing: Trade Space for Time
units.tagline: “Have I seen this?” in O(1), and everything that follows from it.
units.why:
The commonest reason code is quadratic is that it searches. *For each element,
look through the rest* is two nested loops, and the inner one is almost always
asking a question a hash table can answer instantly: **have I seen this value,
and if so, where or how often?**

Hashing is the single highest-return pattern in this curriculum. It turns a
whole tier of O(n²) solutions into O(n) with a few lines, and the cost is memory
— which is nearly always the right trade.
units.model:
### Three structures, three questions

| You need to know | Use | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Have I seen x?* | `HashSet<T>` | O(1) add / contains |
| *How many times have I seen x?* | `HashMap<T, Integer>` | O(1) get / put |
| *Where did I see x?* | `HashMap<T, Integer>` value = index | O(1) |

All three are the same structure underneath. Choosing is just naming what the
value means.

### The complement trick

Two-sum is the archetype, and it generalises: **as you scan, ask whether the
partner you need has already gone past.**

```java
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    int need = target - a[i];
    if (seen.containsKey(need)) return new int[]{ seen.get(need), i };
    seen.put(a[i], i);          // AFTER the check, never before
}
```

Checking before inserting is what stops an element pairing with itself. That one
line ordering is the whole difference between right and wrong.

### Canonical forms

*Group the anagrams* is the same question as *are these equal?* once you can
reduce each item to a **canonical form** — a representative that is identical
for everything in a group. Sorted letters (`"eat"` → `"aet"`) is one; a
26-length count signature is another, and is O(n) rather than O(n log n).

The pattern is worth naming because it is how you hash something that is not
already a key: reduce it to something equal-when-equivalent, then hash *that*.

### Counting when the keys are small

If the keys are letters or small integers, an `int[]` beats a `HashMap` on every
axis — no boxing, no hashing, cache friendly:

```java
int[] freq = new int[26];
freq[c - 'a']++;
```

Reach for the map only when the key space is large or not an integer.
units.internals:
### What `HashMap` actually is

A **bucket array**, plus a rule for turning a key into an index into it.

```
hash = key.hashCode()
hash ^= (hash >>> 16)          // spread the high bits down
index = hash & (table.length - 1)   // cheap modulo, because length is a power of 2
```

Each bucket holds the entries whose keys landed on that index — a **collision**.
Java keeps them in a short linked list, and once a single bucket reaches **8**
entries (with a table of at least 64) it converts that list into a red-black
tree, so a pathological bucket degrades to O(log k) rather than O(k). That is
the entire reason `get` can be called O(1) with a straight face: the average
bucket is tiny, and the worst bucket is bounded.

### Load factor, and why the cost is *amortised*

`HashMap` grows when `size > capacity × 0.75`. Growing means allocating a table
of twice the length and re-indexing **every** entry, because the index depends
on `table.length`. That single insert costs O(n).

Spread over the n inserts that led to it, the cost per insert is still O(1) —
the same amortisation argument as `ArrayList` growth. It is worth being able to
say out loud, because "insert is O(1)" is false about *that* insert and true
about the sequence.

If you know the final size, `new HashMap<>(expectedSize / 0.75f + 1)` skips the
resizes entirely. Rarely decisive, occasionally the difference between passing
and timing out on 10⁶ insertions.

### What `HashMap` does *not* promise

**Any order at all.** Not insertion order, not key order, and not a stable
order across runs or across JDK versions. Code that iterates a `HashMap` and
prints is code whose output is not specified, and the judge compares text — so
this is a correctness bug, not a style one.

When order matters, say which order you mean:

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| insertion order | `LinkedHashMap` |
| sorted by key | `TreeMap` — O(log n) per op, not O(1) |
| no order, fastest | `HashMap` |

### `hashCode` and `equals` are a pair

Two keys that are `equals` **must** have the same `hashCode`, or the map will
store both and find neither reliably. Java's `Integer`, `Long`, `String` and
`List` all honour this. A custom key class that overrides `equals` and forgets
`hashCode` is the classic silent bug — and an `int[]` used as a key is the same
bug with no override in sight, because arrays hash by identity. Use a
`List<Integer>` or a joined string instead.

signals.why: `add` returning false *is* the duplicate test.
Look for `target - x` among what you have already passed.
Sorted letters or a count signature makes equivalent items share a key.
Count in one pass, decide in a second.
Membership tests replace sorting; only extend from a run's first element.

signals.when: Keys are letters or values ≤ a few thousand
signals.why: Same algorithm without boxing, hashing or allocation.

skeletons.name: Seen-set
skeletons.when: Duplicates, first repeat, membership.
skeletons.note: `add` reports novelty and inserts in one operation — no separate `contains`.

skeletons.name: Complement lookup
skeletons.when: Two-sum and every variation of “find the partner”.
skeletons.note: Check, then insert. Inserting first lets an element pair with itself.

skeletons.name: Frequency map
skeletons.when: Counting, majority, top-k, anagram checks.
skeletons.code:
Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
for (int x : a) freq.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);
skeletons.note: `merge` replaces the `getOrDefault(x, 0) + 1` dance.

skeletons.name: Canonical key
skeletons.when: Grouping items that are equivalent under some transformation.
skeletons.note: A 26-int count signature is the O(n) alternative to sorting each word.

skeletons.name: Longest consecutive run
skeletons.when: Sequence problems where sorting would be too slow.
skeletons.note: The `continue` is what keeps it O(n): each run is walked exactly once.

traces.title: Two-sum with a map: nums [3, 8, 11, 4, 7], target 15
traces.intro: For each value, ask the map whether its partner `target − x` has already been seen, *then* add the value. The map holds value → index.
traces.takeaway: Four lookups, and the pair (11, 4) is found at the moment its second half arrives. Checking before inserting is what stops a value pairing with itself — with target 8, x = 4 must not find its own entry.

traces.title: A hash map with 4 buckets, filling up and resizing
traces.intro: Index is `key % capacity`. Two keys landing on one index is a **collision**, and they chain in that bucket. The table doubles once it is more than 75% full.
traces.takeaway: Two things the costs depend on are visible here. **Collisions are normal**, not failures — 7 and 11 share bucket 3 and both are still found, just with one extra comparison; O(1) is average, and it degrades exactly as buckets get long. And a **resize cannot copy buckets across**: an entry's index is `key % capacity`, so doubling the table moves almost everything. That O(n) rehash is why insertion is O(1) *amortized* rather than O(1) — the same doubling argument as `ArrayList`.

costs.note: Worst case O(n) on adversarial keys; not a concern for these problems.
When the key space is a fixed alphabet.
m = item length. The count-signature version drops the log.

pitfalls.symptom: Two-sum returns the same index twice
pitfalls.cause: The current element was inserted into the map before the complement check.
pitfalls.fix: Always check first, insert afterwards.

pitfalls.symptom: `map.get(k)` throws a `NullPointerException`
pitfalls.cause: A missing key returns `null`, which unboxes to an NPE when assigned to `int`.
pitfalls.fix: `map.getOrDefault(k, 0)`, or hold the result in an `Integer` and test for null.

pitfalls.symptom: Counting with `HashMap` is unexpectedly slow
pitfalls.cause: Boxing every `int` into an `Integer` allocates on the hot path.
pitfalls.fix: When keys are bounded and small, use an `int[]` instead.

pitfalls.symptom: Objects that should be equal end up in different buckets
pitfalls.cause: A custom key class overrides `equals` but not `hashCode`.
pitfalls.fix: Override both, or use an already-hashable canonical form such as a `String`.

pitfalls.symptom: Longest-consecutive degrades to O(n²)
pitfalls.cause: Every element walks its whole run, instead of only run starts doing so.
pitfalls.fix: Skip any `x` where `x - 1` is present.

checks.q: Why check the map before inserting the current element in two-sum?
checks.a: Otherwise `target - a[i] == a[i]` finds the element itself and reports a pair of one element with itself.

checks.q: When is `int[26]` better than `HashMap<Character, Integer>`?
checks.a: Whenever the keys are a fixed small alphabet: no boxing, no hashing, better cache behaviour, and O(1) space by definition.

checks.q: Longest-consecutive uses a set and still claims O(n). How?
checks.a: Each run is walked only from its smallest element — guarded by `if (set.contains(x - 1)) continue;` — so every value is visited a constant number of times overall.

checks.q: What makes a good canonical key for grouping anagrams?
checks.a: Anything identical for equivalent items: sorted characters (O(m log m)) or a 26-slot count signature rendered as a string (O(m)).

checks.q: What is the worst-case complexity of a `HashMap` lookup, and why is it acceptable?
checks.a: O(n) if every key collides. With well-distributed hashes it is O(1) average, and Java's map switches long buckets to trees, capping it at O(log n).

checks.q: Why must the map be queried before the new element is inserted?
checks.a: Because the query is what makes every answer refer to an index strictly before the current one. Insert first and an element can pair with itself — target 6 on [3, 1] would report [0, 0]. The rule people memorise as “query before insert” is the loop invariant.

checks.q: When is an `int[26]` the better choice over a `HashMap`?
checks.a: Whenever the key space is small and fixed — lowercase letters, digits, bounded small integers. Same O(n) bound, a much smaller constant, no boxing and no rehashing. The map earns its place when the keys are open-ended.

checks.q: What makes a canonical key safe to group by?
checks.a: That it is injective **by construction**: two different items must not be able to produce it. A sorted string or a 26-slot count signature qualifies; a sum of character codes does not, because `ad` and `bc` both make 199.

checks.q: Why is a hash lookup described as O(1) *average* rather than just O(1)?
checks.a: Because the bound depends on the keys spreading across buckets. With every key colliding, a bucket is a list and a lookup is O(n) — Java caps that at O(log n) by turning long buckets into trees, but the honest statement is still “average”.

bigo.why: One lookup and one insert per element, both O(1) on average. The nested-loop version asks the same question by scanning — and note the space went the other way, O(1) to O(n).
The sort is inside the loop, so it is paid per word. Replacing the key with a 26-slot count signature makes each key O(m) and the whole pass O(n·m) — the same grouping, a cheaper canonical form.

bigo.code:
Map<Character, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();   // fixed 26-letter alphabet
for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) freq.merge(ch, 1, Integer::sum);
options: O(m log m) time, O(1) space
bigo.why: The map holds at most 26 entries whatever m is, so the space is bounded by the **alphabet** and not by the input — a constant, however large it feels. An `int[26]` is the same bound with a far smaller constant and no boxing.
`contains` and `add` are expected O(1), so one pass is O(n) — against O(n²) for checking every pair. "Expected" matters: it assumes a reasonable hash function, which `Integer` has.

bigo.code:
Map<String, Integer> freq = new TreeMap<>();
for (String w : words) freq.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);   // n words
bigo.why: `TreeMap` is a red-black tree: every `merge` is O(log n). You pay for keeping the keys sorted. A `HashMap` counts the same words in O(n) — reach for `TreeMap` only when you need the order. (Word length is treated as bounded here.)
Sorting each word is O(k log k) and dominates; hashing the key is another O(k). String keys are never O(1) to hash — they are O(length). A 26-slot count array as the key brings it to O(n·k).

bigo.code:
for (int x : a)                           // a has n elements
    if (map.containsValue(x)) hits++;     // map has n entries
bigo.why: Only *keys* are hashed. `containsValue` walks every entry, so this is a linear scan inside a loop. If you need to look values up, keep a second map keyed by value.
An array indexed by the character *is* a hash table with a perfect hash. The second loop is a constant 26, and `toCharArray` is a hidden O(n) copy — use `charAt` if the extra memory matters.

units.interview:
Hashing is the expected answer often enough that the interesting follow-up is
always *"now do it without extra space"*. That is your cue to look for sorting,
two pointers, or an in-place marking trick — and to say out loud what you are
giving up: sorting costs O(n log n), and marking usually destroys the input.
