Beware of repeated and leading spaces when counting manually.

skeletons.name: Character frequency
skeletons.when: Anagrams, unique characters, counting letters.
skeletons.code:
int[] freq = new int[26];
for (char c : s.toCharArray()) freq[c - 'a']++;
skeletons.note: Use `int[128]` when the input is not guaranteed lowercase ASCII letters.

skeletons.name: Build with StringBuilder
skeletons.when: Any output longer than a single value.
skeletons.note: One allocation, one print — instead of n of each.

skeletons.name: Run-length scan
skeletons.when: Compression, longest run of a character, grouping neighbours.
skeletons.note: The outer `for` has no increment — the inner loop is what advances `i`.

skeletons.name: Vertical scan for a common prefix
skeletons.when: Longest common prefix across many strings.
skeletons.note: Compare column by column; stop at the first disagreement.

skeletons.name: Expand around centre
skeletons.when: Count palindromic substrings, or find the longest.
skeletons.note: After the loop, `l` and `r` are one step past the palindrome: its length is r − l − 1.

skeletons.name: KMP search
skeletons.when: First (or every) occurrence of a pattern in O(n + m).
skeletons.note: Building `pi` is the same loop as searching — the pattern matched against itself.

traces.title: Run-length encoding "aaabccdddd"
traces.intro: Find the run starting at `i` by advancing `j` while the character repeats, emit the character and its length, then jump `i` straight to `j`.
traces.takeaway: Four runs, ten characters, and `i` jumps to `j` each time, so every character is examined once — O(n). Setting `i++` instead of `i = j` would still produce the right first piece and then re-encode the tail of every run. Build the output with a `StringBuilder` in Java; the column is a string here only to show its state.

traces.title: Every palindrome in "abaab", by expanding around 2m − 1 centres
traces.intro: A palindrome is symmetric about a centre, and that centre is either a letter (odd length) or the gap between two letters (even length). Five letters means **nine** centres, not five.
traces.takeaway: 8 palindromic substrings. The `aa` at centre 5 is the row that matters: it sits between two letters, so expanding only from letters would never find it — and the bug shows up as an answer that is right on every odd-length example. Each expansion costs O(m) in the worst case, so the whole scan is O(m²) with O(1) space, which is the trade against building a table.

costs.note: The canonical form for anagram grouping — count signatures are O(n).
Checking every substring separately is O(n³).

pitfalls.symptom: String building is inexplicably slow on large input
pitfalls.cause: `s += x` inside a loop allocates and copies the whole string each iteration.
pitfalls.fix: Use `StringBuilder` and convert once at the end.

pitfalls.symptom: `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` in a frequency array
pitfalls.cause: `c - 'a'` on an uppercase letter, a digit or a space gives a negative or out-of-range index.
pitfalls.fix: Use `int[128]` indexed by the raw char, or normalise the case first.

pitfalls.symptom: Two identical-looking strings compare as different
pitfalls.cause: `==` compares references. Literals may be interned, which makes it work sometimes — the worst possible failure mode.
pitfalls.fix: Always `equals`.

pitfalls.symptom: The word count is one too high
pitfalls.cause: Splitting on a single space counts empty tokens from repeated or leading spaces.
pitfalls.fix: Count transitions from space to non-space, or split on `\s+` after trimming.

pitfalls.symptom: A substring comparison loop is O(n³)
pitfalls.cause: Each `substring` call copies before the comparison even starts.
pitfalls.fix: Compare with `charAt` in place, or use indices rather than copies.

pitfalls.symptom: Even-length palindromes are missing
pitfalls.cause: Only the n letters were used as centres, not the n − 1 gaps.
pitfalls.fix: Loop over 2n − 1 centres: `l = c / 2, r = l + c % 2`.

pitfalls.symptom: KMP is still O(n · m), or misses overlapping matches
pitfalls.cause: On a mismatch `k` was reset to 0, or after a full match it was not set to `pi[k − 1]`.
pitfalls.fix: Fall back through `pi`; after a match continue from `k = pi[m − 1]`.

checks.q: Why is `result += c` inside a loop O(n²)?
checks.a: `String` is immutable, so each `+=` allocates a new string and copies everything built so far. Summed over n iterations that is quadratic.

checks.q: What does `c - 'a'` give you, and when is it wrong?
checks.a: The 0-based index of a lowercase letter. It is wrong — silently negative or too large — for uppercase letters, digits, spaces or punctuation.

checks.q: Is `s.substring(i, j)` O(1)?
checks.a: No. Modern Java copies the range, so it is O(j − i). A loop of substrings is a hidden extra factor of n.

checks.q: Two ways to test whether two words are anagrams — and their costs?
checks.a: Sort both and compare: O(n log n). Count characters into `int[26]` and compare the tables: O(n). The second is preferred and also generalises to grouping.

checks.q: Why are there 2n − 1 centres for palindromes, not n?
checks.a: Odd-length palindromes centre on a letter; even-length ones centre on the gap between two letters. n letters plus n − 1 gaps.

checks.q: What does the KMP prefix function store, and why does it make the search linear?
checks.a: pi[i] is the longest proper prefix of t[0..i] that is also its suffix. On a mismatch the search falls back to that border instead of restarting, so the text pointer never moves back and k falls at most as often as it rose.

checks.q: Why does expanding around centres use `2m - 1` centres and not m?
checks.a: Because an even-length palindrome is symmetric about the **gap** between two characters, not about a character. Expanding only from characters finds `aba` and misses `abba` — and the bug produces correct answers on every odd-length example.

checks.q: `s.substring(i, i + m).equals(t)` versus `s.regionMatches(i, t, 0, m)` — what changes?
checks.a: Not the complexity: both are O(n·m) in the worst case. `substring` **copies** m characters on every iteration and then throws them away; `regionMatches` compares in place. The habit worth building is asking whether you need the substring or only need to compare it.

checks.q: Why is summing character codes a bad key for grouping anagrams?
checks.a: It is not injective: `ad` and `bc` both sum to 199, so they would be grouped together. A canonical key has to be collision-free by construction — sort the characters, or use a 26-slot count signature.

checks.q: Why does the run-length scan's outer `for` have an empty increment clause?
checks.a: Because the inner loop is what advances the index, past the whole run. Leaving `i++` in as well skips the first character of every run after the first, and the output is wrong only where runs repeat.

bigo.code:
String out = "";                                  // n parts
for (String part : parts) out += part;
bigo.why: Java strings are immutable, so `+=` allocates and copies everything accumulated so far: 1 + 2 + 3 + … characters. Quadratic **in the total length**, from a loop that reads as linear. `StringBuilder` makes it O(n) amortized.

bigo.code:
for (int i = 0; i + m <= n; i++)                  // text n, pattern m
    if (s.substring(i, i + m).equals(t)) return i;
bigo.why: Two costs of the same order, and one of them is invisible: `substring` **copies** m characters before `equals` compares them. `regionMatches` removes the allocation without changing the bound; KMP removes the bound, at O(n + m).
2m − 1 centres, each expanding up to m/2 steps — `aaaa…a` reaches the bound. O(1) space, which is the trade against a DP table. Manacher does the same job in O(m) and is rarely expected.

bigo.code:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)               // s has n chars, p has m ≤ n
    if (s.substring(i).startsWith(p)) count++;
bigo.why: `substring` copies — since Java 7 it allocates a new array of n − i characters — so the copying alone is 1 + 2 + … + n. `s.startsWith(p, i)` compares in place and makes it O(n·m).

bigo.code:
for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++)
    if (s.toCharArray()[i] == 'a') count++;
bigo.why: `toCharArray` copies the entire string, and it is called once per character. Hoist the copy above the loop, or use `charAt(i)`, and it is O(n).

bigo.code: boolean pal = new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString().equals(s);
bigo.why: Three linear passes — copy into the builder, reverse, copy out and compare — is still O(n). Two pointers from the ends do it in one pass with no extra memory, which is a space win rather than a time one.
The anagram check by sorting. It is correct and short, and a 26-slot count array does it in O(n) — the difference an interviewer is usually fishing for.

bigo.code:
for (String w : words)                    // m words, each ≤ k chars
    if (text.indexOf(w) >= 0) found++;    // text has n chars
bigo.why: `String.indexOf` is a naive search: O(n·k) in the worst case, per word. Real text rarely hits the worst case, which is why this is usually fast and occasionally a timeout. A trie or Aho–Corasick shares the work across words.

units.interview:
String questions are rarely about strings — they are array questions wearing a
costume, plus one Java-specific trap the interviewer is watching for. Reaching
for `StringBuilder` unprompted, and saying "`substring` copies, so I will
compare in place", both register as production instincts rather than
competitive-programming ones.

units.build_it:
### Write the string toolkit without the convenience methods

The rule for this exercise: **no `substring`, no `split`, no `+` on strings
inside a loop.** Everything with `charAt`, indices and one `StringBuilder`.

**1. `reverseWords(String s)`** — collapse runs of spaces, no leading or
trailing space in the output. Do it by scanning word boundaries as index pairs
and appending, never by `split(" ")`. Then answer: what does `split(" ")` return
for `"a  b"`, and why is that a bug and not a preference?

**2. `isPalindrome(String s)`** ignoring case and non-alphanumerics, with two
pointers and no cleaned copy of the input. The skipping belongs in the `while`
conditions; if you built a filtered string first, you used O(m) space to avoid
two `if`s.

**3. `runLengthEncode(String s)`.** Outer `for` with an **empty** increment
clause, inner `while` consuming the run. Then encode a string of 10⁵ identical
characters and check the output is `a100000`, not `a1` repeated — that is the
test that catches the stray `i++`.

**4. `longestCommonPrefix(String[] words)`** by vertical scan: column 0 across
every word, then column 1, stopping at the first mismatch or the first word that
ends. Compare against the version that shortens a candidate with `substring` in
a loop, on 10⁴ words of length 100, and time both.

**5. `countPalindromicSubstrings(String s)`** by expanding around all `2m - 1`
centres. Write the centre loop before the expansion helper — getting `2m - 1`
right is the exercise, and the check is that `"abba"` reports 6, not 4.

**6. Build the KMP prefix function** for `"aabaaab"` **by hand on paper first**,
then write the loop and compare. The falling-back line
(`while (k > 0 && s.charAt(i) != s.charAt(k)) k = pi[k - 1];`) is the one that
cannot be reconstructed from intuition, and doing it on paper once is what makes
it stick.

Then use it twice: to find a pattern, and to report the smallest period as
`n - pi[n - 1]`. Two answers from one array is the reason the technique earns
its place.
units.next_up:
That is the pattern toolkit for linear data. The next stage adds **order** —
sorting, binary search, and the greedy rules that sorted data makes provable —
starting with the recursion that the best sorting ideas are built on.

variants.name: Frequency signature
variants.change: Reduce the string to 26 counts and compare those instead of the characters.
variants.when: Anagrams, “same letters”, permutation-in-string.
variants.gotcha: Only valid for a **fixed** alphabet. On Unicode, or on arbitrary tokens, it becomes a `HashMap` and you lose the constant factor, not the bound.

variants.name: Canonical form as a key
variants.change: Map each string to one normal form and group by it.
variants.when: Group anagrams, “which of these are the same word”.
variants.cost: O(n · m log m) sorting each, or O(n · m) with count signatures
variants.gotcha: The key must be injective by construction. Summing character codes is the classic wrong key: `ad` and `bc` both make 199.

variants.name: Two pointers over one string
variants.change: Walk from both ends, skipping what the problem says to ignore.
variants.when: Palindromes, “valid after removing non-alphanumerics”, reversing words.
variants.gotcha: Skipping in the *condition* rather than the body is what keeps it one loop: `while (l < r && !isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(l))) l++;`

variants.name: Expand around a centre
variants.change: For each of the `2m - 1` centres, grow outwards while the sides match.
variants.when: Longest palindromic substring, counting palindromic substrings.
variants.gotcha: `2m - 1` centres, not m — even-length palindromes sit *between* two characters. Expanding only from characters silently misses `abba`.

variants.name: Run-length scan
variants.change: An outer loop with no increment; an inner loop that consumes a whole run and advances the index.
variants.when: Compression, longest run, grouping equal neighbours.
variants.gotcha: The outer `for` must have an empty increment clause. Leaving `i++` in as well skips the first character of every run after the first.

variants.name: Vertical scan across many strings
variants.change: Iterate by *column* across all n strings rather than string by string.
variants.when: Longest common prefix.
variants.cost: O(total characters), and it stops early
variants.gotcha: No substring is ever built, so there are no copies — the version that repeatedly shortens a candidate prefix with `substring` is O(n · m) in copying alone.

variants.name: Prefix function (KMP)
variants.change: Precompute the longest border of every prefix, then never move the text pointer backwards.
variants.when: Finding a pattern, periodicity, “is this a repeated block”.
variants.gotcha: The same loop builds `pi` and runs the search. If you have written it twice, you have written it once too often.

rewrites.title: Comparing substrings
rewrites.edit: `substring(...).equals(t)` becomes `regionMatches`, which compares in place.
rewrites.why:
Both versions are O(n·m) in the worst case, and this rewrite is still worth
making — which is the useful lesson, because not every improvement is a
complexity class.

`substring` **copies**. Since Java 7 it allocates a fresh character array, so
the slow version does up to n allocations of m characters each and then throws
them all away. `regionMatches` compares the two ranges where they already are.

The habit to build is *"do I need this substring, or do I need to compare it?"*.
The same question retires most `split`/`substring`/`trim` chains in a hot loop.

For the genuine complexity win on this exact problem, the answer is the KMP
prefix function — O(n + m) by never moving the text pointer backwards. That is
in the `strings` playbook and again in the optional string-matching unit.

rewrites.title: Are these two strings anagrams
rewrites.edit: Two sorts become one pass over both strings, sharing a single counter array.
rewrites.why:
Sorting builds a total order and then uses only the equality test. The question
is "same multiset of letters", and the cheapest canonical form for a multiset is
the multiset — 26 counters.

The single-array trick is the part worth stealing: rather than building two
frequency arrays and comparing them, increment for one string and decrement for
the other. Equal multisets leave every counter at zero, so the comparison is a
scan of 26 values and the second array never exists.

The length guard is load-bearing, not defensive: the loop uses one index for
both strings and would read out of bounds without it.

Bound alphabet, bound win. On Unicode or arbitrary tokens this becomes a
`HashMap` and stays O(m) with a much larger constant — still better than
sorting, and worth saying which part of the improvement survives.

stages.title: Order & Search
stages.goal:
Sorting costs O(n log n) and buys you an enormous amount: binary search, two
pointers, greedy sweeps, duplicate detection and interval merging all become
available the moment the data is in order. This stage is about knowing what
that purchase is worth and when to make it.

| Unit | What order buys it |
| --- | --- |
| **Recursion** | Nothing yet — it is the notation merge sort and quickselect are written in |
| **Sorting** | Equal things adjacent, extremes at the ends, and pairs that can be *counted* while merging |
| **Binary search** | One comparison discards half — over an array, or over the answer itself |
| **Greedy** | A processing order in which the best local move is provably safe |
| **Intervals** | Overlaps that can only happen between neighbours |

It opens with **recursion**, because the sorts worth understanding are
recursive: merge sort splits and merges, quickselect partitions and recurses
into one side. It closes with **greedy** and **intervals** — the families where
"sort, then take the best local move" is provably right, and where you learn
to check that it is.

**The hard part is the near misses.** *k-th largest* is a sort, a heap or a
quickselect depending on k and on whether you need the rest of the order.
*Minimum X such that it works* is binary search on the answer — unless
"works" is not monotone. *Maximum non-overlapping* is greedy by end time — until
each interval carries a **weight**, and then it is dynamic programming. The
routing table below is those boundaries, written down.

router.when: “sort by …”, “order by frequency / a second key / a custom rule”
router.why: A comparator, built from `comparingInt` and `thenComparing`. The rule is the whole problem.
router.not_when: If the rule compares *pairs* (“which of these two goes first?”) and has no key, the ordering itself needs an exchange argument — that is greedy.

router.when: “k-th largest / smallest”, one value
router.why: Quickselect: O(n) average, recurses into one side of a partition.
router.not_when: The **top k** as a set, or k-th in a *stream*, is a size-k heap (heaps unit). k-th in a sorted *matrix* or a multiplication table is binary search over values.

router.when: “how many pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]” (or `> 2·a[j]`, …)
router.why: Merge sort counts every cross-midpoint pair at the merge, in O(n log n) total.
router.not_when: Pairs with a *sum* condition in sorted data are two pointers (stage 2).

router.when: Values are small integers, or fixed-width keys
router.why: Counting or radix sort: O(n + k) or O(d·n), with no comparisons at all.
router.not_when: Arbitrary 64-bit values with no bound — the comparison sort is simpler and just as fast in practice.

router.when: “sorted array” + find / insert position / count / first ≥ x
router.why: Lower bound. One half-open template answers all four questions.
router.not_when: Unsorted data queried once — a linear scan is O(n) and sorting first is O(n log n).

router.when: “minimum capacity / speed / days / time such that it is possible”
router.why: Binary search on the answer: `feasible(x)` is easy to check and monotone in x.
router.not_when: If feasibility is **not** monotone (possible at 5, impossible at 6), the search is invalid — usually that is DP.

router.when: “maximise the minimum distance / gap / share”
router.why: The mirror image: the *largest* x that is still feasible. Same loop, the other branch keeps `mid`.

router.when: “k-th smallest” over a space too big to list (pair distances, a table)
router.why: Search the *value*: count how many are ≤ x, and find the first x whose count reaches k.
router.not_when: If the space is small enough to generate, a heap or quickselect is simpler.

router.when: A rotated sorted array, a peak, a bitonic sequence
router.why: No global order, but one comparison still tells you which half to keep.
router.not_when: With **duplicates**, that comparison can be inconclusive and the worst case degrades to O(n).

router.when: “recursion”, “in terms of a smaller input”, a tree or nested structure
router.why: Write the one-sentence promise, the base case, and the combine.
router.not_when: If the same arguments recur on different branches, it is DP — memoise.

router.when: “split, solve both halves, combine” — a crossing term
router.why: Divide and conquer. The work is the combine step across the midpoint.

router.when: “maximum profit / furthest reach / fewest jumps”, one pass
router.why: A running extreme or a furthest reach — the stays-ahead argument.
router.not_when: When a worse move now can pay off later (coins {1, 3, 4}), greedy is wrong. Find the counterexample, then write the DP.

router.when: “in what order should the jobs run” to minimise a total or a lateness
router.why: Exchange argument: compare two adjacent jobs, and sort by whichever order the swap proves is never worse.
router.not_when: Jobs with deadlines **and** profits, where some may be skipped, still greedy — but the slot choice needs care (latest free slot).

router.when: “merge overlapping”, “insert into a schedule”, “total covered length”
router.why: Sort by **start** and build left to right; only the last merged block can overlap the next.
router.not_when: Keeping the most intervals is the other sort — by **end**.

router.when: “maximum non-overlapping”, “fewest removals / arrows”
router.why: Sort by **end**, keep greedily. The earliest finish leaves the most room.
router.not_when: Each interval has a **weight** and you maximise total weight: greedy fails. Sort by end, binary-search the predecessor, and DP.

router.when: “minimum rooms / platforms”, “busiest moment”
router.why: Peak concurrency: a ±1 sweep over sorted events, or a min-heap of ends.
router.not_when: Release before you allocate at equal timestamps, or the peak is one too high.

units.title: Recursion
units.tagline: Trust the smaller call. Every branching technique depends on it.
units.why:
Recursion is not a technique for a family of problems; it is the *notation*
every remaining unit is written in. Tree traversal, backtracking, DFS, divide
and conquer and the top-down half of dynamic programming are all one pattern:
express the answer in terms of the same function on a smaller input.

The block people hit is almost never syntax. It is refusing to **trust the
recursive call** — trying to trace the whole stack in their head instead of
assuming the smaller call is already correct and asking only what to do with its
result.
units.model:
### The contract

Write a recursive function by answering three questions, in this order:

1. **What does this function promise?** One sentence, for *any* valid input.
   "`depth(node)` returns the height of the subtree rooted at `node`." If you
   cannot write that sentence, no amount of tracing will help.
2. **Base case.** The smallest input, answered without recursion. It is almost
   always `null`, empty, or zero — and it is almost always where the bug is.
3. **Recursive case.** Assume the promise holds for smaller inputs. Call, and
   combine. Do not trace.

```java
static int depth(Node node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;                       // base
    return 1 + Math.max(depth(node.left), depth(node.right));   // combine
}
```

### The cost

Each call keeps a stack frame, so a recursion n deep costs O(n) **memory** even
if it allocates nothing. Java's default stack overflows around 10,000 frames —
which is why a recursive walk over a 10⁵-long linked list crashes and an
iterative one does not.

The time cost comes from the recurrence:

| Recurrence | Solves to | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `T(n) = T(n−1) + O(1)` | O(n) | Walking a list |
| `T(n) = 2T(n−1) + O(1)` | O(2ⁿ) | Naive Fibonacci |
| `T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)` | O(log n) | Binary search, fast power |
| `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)` | O(n log n) | Merge sort |

### Halving

Fast exponentiation makes one call on half the exponent:

```java
static long power(long b, long e) {
    if (e == 0) return 1;
    long half = power(b, e / 2);      // ONE call, not two
    return (e % 2 == 0) ? half * half : half * half * b;
}
```

Calling `power(b, e/2)` twice instead of storing it turns O(log e) into O(e).
That single line is the difference, and it is the same insight as memoisation:
never compute the same thing twice.

### Divide and conquer

Split into **independent** parts, solve each, combine. Merge sort is the
canonical example, and the one the sorting unit builds on:

```java
static void sort(int[] a, int[] buf, int lo, int hi) {   // sorts [lo, hi)
    if (hi - lo < 2) return;                             // base: 0 or 1 element
    int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
    sort(a, buf, lo, mid);                               // trust it
    sort(a, buf, mid, hi);                               // trust it
    merge(a, buf, lo, mid, hi);                          // two-pointer merge, O(n)
}
```

Read the cost off the code: two calls on halves plus linear work is
`T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)`. The recursion tree has log n levels and the merges on
each level touch every element once, so the total is O(n log n).

The halves do not have to be halves. *Different ways to add parentheses* splits
at every operator, solves both sides, and combines every pair of results — the
same three steps with a different split.

### When recursion repeats itself

Naive Fibonacci is O(2ⁿ) because `fib(n−2)` is recomputed on both branches. Two
fixes, and the whole DP stage is built on them:

- **Memoise**: cache each answer by argument. Top-down DP.
- **Iterate**: compute the small answers first. Bottom-up DP.

Recognising the overlap is the skill. The DP unit later is this observation with
a syllabus attached.

### Reading the cost: the Master theorem

Most divide-and-conquer recurrences have the shape `T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n)`:
`a` subproblems, each `1/b` the size, plus `f(n)` work to split and combine.
Compare `f(n)` with `n^(log_b a)`, the number of leaves in the recursion tree:

| Case | Who wins | Result | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `f(n)` smaller | The leaves | `O(n^(log_b a))` | `T = 4T(n/2) + n` → O(n²) |
| Equal | Every level ties | `O(n^(log_b a) · log n)` | Merge sort, `2T(n/2) + n` → O(n log n) |
| `f(n)` larger | The root | `O(f(n))` | `T = 2T(n/2) + n²` → O(n²) |

You rarely need the formal statement. The picture is enough: **total work = sum
over levels**, and you only have to decide whether the levels shrink, stay
level, or grow as you go down.

### Divide and conquer beyond sorting

The interesting part of a divide and conquer is never the split; it is the
**answer that straddles the midpoint**. Maximum subarray by halves: the best
subarray is entirely in the left half, entirely in the right, or it *crosses the
middle* — and the crossing one is the best suffix of the left glued to the best
prefix of the right, found in O(n). So `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)` = O(n log n).

Closest pair of points, counting inversions and the majority element by halves
all have the same shape: two recursive calls you trust, and one linear pass that
handles the pairs neither call could see.
units.internals:
### What a call actually costs

Every call pushes a **frame** onto the thread's stack: the return address, the
parameters, and every local variable. It is popped when the call returns. A
frame for a small method is tens of bytes; the default Java thread stack is
typically 512 KB–1 MB, set by `-Xss`. That puts the practical depth limit at
**about 10⁴ frames**, and less when frames are fat.

Nothing in the algorithm's Big-O mentions this, which is why it catches people:
a DFS over a 10⁵-node path graph is O(n) time and still crashes.

### Three ways out

1. **Rewrite as a loop** — whenever the work after the call is trivial (see the
   rewrites above).
2. **An explicit stack** — a `Deque<Frame>` on the heap, which holds millions of
   entries. This is how iterative DFS and iterative in-order traversal work.
3. **Run on a thread with a bigger stack** — the competitive-programming
   escape hatch:

```java
new Thread(null, () -> solve(), "main", 1 << 26).start();   // 64 MB stack
```

Correct, and occasionally the pragmatic answer, but in an interview say option
1 or 2 first.

### No tail calls in Java

A call is a *tail call* when nothing happens after it returns:
`return helper(n - 1, acc * n);`. Some languages reuse the frame for tail calls,
making such recursion O(1) space. **The JVM does not.** Writing a function in
tail-recursive style in Java changes nothing about its stack depth — it only
makes the conversion to a loop mechanical.

### Memoisation's hidden cost

A `HashMap<Long, Long>` memo boxes both key and value and hashes on every
lookup — roughly 10× slower than a `long[]` indexed by the argument. When the
arguments are small integers, use an array; when they are a pair `(i, j)`, use
a 2-D array; reach for a map only when the argument space is sparse or not an
integer range.

signals.when: “the same problem on a smaller input”
signals.why: Subtrees, suffixes, “with one more item chosen”.
The structure is already recursive; mirror it.
Two independent halves, then a merge step.

signals.when: Exponent or range halves each step
signals.why: Compute the half once and reuse it.

signals.when: The same sub-input recurs on different branches
signals.why: Overlapping subproblems is the definition of DP.
The call stack, not the algorithm, is what will fail.

skeletons.name: The three-part shape
skeletons.when: Every recursive function you will write from here on.
skeletons.note: Write the one-sentence promise above the function before the body.

skeletons.name: Fast exponentiation
skeletons.when: Powers, matrix powers, repeated doubling.
skeletons.note: Two recursive calls here would make it O(e) instead of O(log e).

skeletons.name: Divide and conquer (merge sort)
skeletons.when: Sort, count across a midpoint, combine independent halves.
skeletons.note: One buffer allocated by the caller. `<=` keeps equal elements in order — that is stability.

skeletons.name: Memoised recursion
skeletons.when: Whenever the same argument recurs across branches.
skeletons.note: O(2ⁿ) → O(n) by adding two lines. This is top-down DP.

traces.title: The call stack of fact(4)
traces.intro: Each call waits on the one it made. The stack column shows every frame alive at that moment, oldest on the left — the rightmost is the one running.
traces.takeaway: The stack grows to four frames before anything is multiplied: all the work happens on the way *back*, as each frame resumes with its child's answer. That depth is the O(n) space cost of recursion, and it is what overflows for n in the tens of thousands.

traces.title: Fast power: power(3, 13), one call per level
traces.intro: Each call halves the exponent and makes **one** recursive call. The odd levels multiply in one extra factor of the base.
traces.takeaway: Thirteen is 1101 in binary, and the chain of calls reads its bits: 13 → 6 → 3 → 1 → 0 is five frames, ⌊log₂ 13⌋ + 2. The odd exponents (13, 3, 1) are exactly the 1-bits. Calling `power(b, e/2)` twice would double the calls at every level: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 calls instead of 5.

traces.title: Maximum subarray by halves on [2, −5, 6, −1, 3, −7, 4, 1]
traces.intro: Each row is one divide-and-conquer node, in the order it *returns* (children first). The crossing column is the best suffix of the left half plus the best prefix of the right — the only part of the answer neither recursive call can see.
traces.takeaway: The winner, 6 − 1 + 3 = 8, lies in neither half: it straddles the midpoint between indices 3 and 4, so neither recursive call at the root can see it. Only the root's crossing term finds it — the best left suffix (6 − 1 = 5) plus the best right prefix (3). Each level does O(n) crossing work over log n levels: O(n log n).

traces.title: Tower of Hanoi, n = 3: which call prints each move
traces.intro: Each row is one printed move, tagged with the call that printed it; the dots are that call's depth. A call prints only *between* its two recursive calls.
traces.takeaway: Seven moves, 2³ − 1. Disk 3 moves exactly once, in the middle, printed by the root; disk 1 moves on every odd step. Read it as the promise, not the trace: move 2 disks out of the way, move disk 3, move 2 disks back on top. No memo can shorten this — the output itself is exponential.

costs.op: Divide and conquer with a linear merge

pitfalls.symptom: `StackOverflowError`
pitfalls.cause: Either no base case, or a legitimate recursion deeper than ~10,000 frames.
pitfalls.fix: Check the base case first; if the depth is genuinely large, rewrite iteratively.

pitfalls.symptom: The base case returns the wrong identity
pitfalls.cause: `return 0` where the combination multiplies, or `return 1` where it sums.
pitfalls.fix: Ask what the answer for an empty input *must* be for the combination to work.

pitfalls.symptom: An exponential runtime in something that looks linear
pitfalls.cause: A sub-answer is recomputed on multiple branches.
pitfalls.fix: Memoise, or restructure so each sub-answer is computed once.

pitfalls.symptom: Fast power is O(e) instead of O(log e)
pitfalls.cause: `power(b, e/2)` was written twice rather than stored.
pitfalls.fix: Call once, store in a local, square it.

pitfalls.symptom: A shared mutable structure leaks between branches
pitfalls.cause: State was modified before the call and never restored after it.
pitfalls.fix: Either pass immutable arguments, or undo the change — see backtracking.

pitfalls.symptom: A divide and conquer is right on small inputs and wrong on large ones
pitfalls.cause: The combine step forgot the answer that crosses the midpoint.
pitfalls.fix: List the three places the answer can be: left, right, straddling. The third is the one you write code for.

pitfalls.symptom: A memoised recursion is still slow
pitfalls.cause: The memo is a `HashMap<String, …>` keyed by a string built on every call, or the sentinel collides with a real answer (0 used as “unset”).
pitfalls.fix: Index an array by the integer arguments; use −1 (or a separate `boolean[]`) as the “not computed” marker.

pitfalls.symptom: The recursion never shrinks on a two-element range
pitfalls.cause: `mid = (lo + hi) / 2` with a recursive call on `[mid, hi]` — when `hi = lo + 1`, that is the same range.
pitfalls.fix: Use half-open ranges and recurse on `[lo, mid)` and `[mid, hi)`; stop at size < 2.

checks.q: What are the three parts of writing a recursive function?
checks.a: A one-sentence promise about what it returns for any input; a base case that needs no recursion; and a recursive case that trusts the promise and combines.

checks.q: Why does naive Fibonacci take exponential time?
checks.a: `fib(n-2)` is recomputed under both `fib(n-1)` and `fib(n-2)`, so the call tree branches twice at nearly every level: T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2).

checks.q: What is the space complexity of a recursion n levels deep that allocates nothing?
checks.a: O(n) — every pending frame stays on the call stack until it returns.

checks.q: Why must fast exponentiation store the half-power in a variable?
checks.a: Calling it twice doubles the work at every level, collapsing O(log e) back to O(e). Storing it is the entire optimisation.

checks.q: Why is merge sort O(n log n), read straight from its code?
checks.a: Two calls on halves plus a linear merge: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). There are log n levels of halving, and the merges on each level handle all n elements once.

checks.q: What does `T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n)` solve to, and why?
checks.a: O(n²). Each level has 4× the calls on half the size, so level work doubles going down: n, 2n, 4n, … The leaves dominate — n^(log₂4) = n² of them.

checks.q: Does writing a Java method in tail-recursive form save stack space?
checks.a: No. The JVM performs no tail-call elimination, so every call still keeps a frame. Tail form only makes the conversion to a loop mechanical.

checks.q: In maximum subarray by halves, what does the combine step compute?
checks.a: The best subarray that *crosses* the midpoint: the best suffix sum of the left half plus the best prefix sum of the right half, in O(n). The answer is the maximum of that and the two recursive results.

checks.q: Tower of Hanoi and naive Fibonacci both make two calls. Why can only one be memoised into polynomial time?
checks.a: Fibonacci's two calls share arguments, so its exponential tree has only n distinct nodes. Hanoi's output — the move list — is itself 2ⁿ − 1 long, so any algorithm that prints it is exponential.

checks.q: When would you choose an explicit stack over recursion?
checks.a: When the depth can reach ~10⁴ or more (a path graph, a degenerate tree, a long list). The algorithm is unchanged; the frames move from the thread stack to the heap.

bigo.why: Memoised, each n is computed once and every later call returns in O(1). Without the memo it is O(φⁿ) ≈ O(1.618ⁿ) — the same code, exponentially apart.

It halves e, which suggests O(log e) — but it recurses *twice* per level. The call tree has log e levels and doubles in width each time: 2^(log e) = e calls. Store `pow(b, e / 2)` in a variable and it really is O(log e).
n calls, and each copies the rest of the array: n + (n−1) + … + 1. Pass an index instead of a slice and it is O(n). Slicing is free in some languages' notation and never free in Java.
2ⁿ leaves, and printing each one costs n characters. The internal nodes add only 2ⁿ more calls. When the output itself is exponential, no algorithm can be faster than its size.
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). Draw the tree: log n levels, and each level's merges touch n elements in total. Counting work *per level* is the reliable way to price a divide-and-conquer recursion.

`T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n`. Level k has 4ᵏ calls of size n/2ᵏ, so it does 2ᵏ·n work — the levels *grow* going down, and the leaves win: n^(log₂4) = n². Merge sort's levels tie because it makes 2 calls, not 4.
`T(n) = T(n/2) + n` = n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n. One call per level means the work shrinks geometrically, and the root's loop dominates. This is quickselect's expected-case shape.
n levels, and each copies a substring and builds a new string of up to n characters: 1 + 2 + … + n. The recursion looks linear; the copying is quadratic. A `char[]` swapped from both ends is O(n).

units.interview:
Interviewers probe recursion by asking for the complexity and then for the
iterative version. Have both ready: the recurrence that gives the time bound,
and the observation that depth is memory. And when a recursive solution is
exponential, say *why* — "the same subproblem appears on both branches, so I
will memoise" is the sentence that turns a rejected answer into an accepted one.

### Say it out loud

- *"Let me state what this function returns for any input: …"* — say the promise
  before the base case.
- *"The recurrence is T(n) = …, which gives O(…)"* — price it from the code.
- *"The same arguments recur on different branches, so I'll memoise on (…)."*
- *"The depth is n, so at 10⁵ I'd convert this to a loop or an explicit stack."*

rungs.title: Warm up
rungs.purpose: Where the work sits relative to the call decides the order it happens in.

notes.to-base-recursive: Append the last digit *after* the recursive call and the digits come out in order. Move the line above the call and watch them reverse.

rungs.title: Core
rungs.purpose: A recurrence you can write in one line.

notes.nth-fibonacci: Write it naively, note it is O(2ⁿ), then memoise. That one edit is the whole DP stage in miniature.
notes.binomial-coefficient: Pascal's rule, word for word. Count the calls for C(20, 10), then ask what C(60, 30) would cost.

rungs.title: Variations
rungs.purpose: Recursion that halves rather than decrements.

notes.fast-power: Store the half-power. Calling twice is the bug that makes it O(e).
notes.mulmod-by-halving: Fast power with × replaced by +. Write the one-line overflow argument — every value stays below 2m — before the code.

rungs.title: Two calls
rungs.purpose: Recursion that branches, where the exponential cost is the answer's own size.

notes.tower-of-hanoi: Trust the smaller call. Then compare with `nth-fibonacci`: both make two calls, and only one of them can be fixed by a memo.

rungs.title: Too deep for the stack
rungs.purpose: A correct recursion n frames deep, and the loop that computes the same thing.

notes.josephus-survivor: The recurrence is one line. Write it recursively, run n = 10⁶, read the StackOverflowError — then compute the same values smallest-first in a loop.

rungs.title: Divide and conquer
rungs.purpose: Split into independent halves, solve both, combine — the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) as code.

notes.merge-sort-array: Trust both recursive calls, then merge with two pointers. Count the levels: log n of them, each merging n elements in total.
notes.closest-pair-points: Trust both halves; the whole algorithm is the strip. Say why each point checks only a handful of neighbours above it.

rungs.title: Extra practice
rungs.purpose: More recursive structure — optional, counted only once started.

notes.find-kth-bit: Answer a point query on a million-character string by following one position down.
notes.permutation-sequence: Each first digit owns (n − 1)! permutations, so division skips whole recursive branches.
notes.elimination-game: Survivors form an arithmetic sequence; halve the problem with head, step and count.
notes.tribonacci: A recurrence with a fixed look-back needs only a fixed window of variables.
notes.pascal-triangle-row: Update one row in place, right to left, so each old value is read before it is overwritten.
notes.count-and-say: A recursive definition whose recursion is a straight chain — so a loop computes it.
notes.nested-list-depth-sum: A recursive descent parser: one call per bracket, and the depth rides along.
notes.unique-paths-count: `paths(i,j) = paths(i-1,j) + paths(i,j-1)`. Same shape, two dimensions.
notes.kth-symbol-grammar: Recurse on the index, not the row: every symbol has one parent, and rows halve on the way up.
notes.gray-code: Two copies of the smaller answer, one reversed. The seam differs by exactly the new bit.
notes.ways-to-add-parentheses: Split at every operator, solve each side into a list of values, combine every pair. Divide and conquer where the halves are not halves.
notes.sierpinski-cell: Recurse on the quadrant the cell is in. Then look at which bits each level tested — the answer collapses to `(r & c) == 0`.

units.build_it:
### Write these from an empty file

**1. `power(b, e, mod)`.** Recursive, then iterative (square the base, halve the
exponent, multiply in when the low bit is set). Check both against a loop for
`e` up to 1000 and against each other for `e = 10¹⁸`.

**2. Merge sort** with one caller-allocated buffer. Then add a counter to the
merge and return the number of inversions — without changing the sort.

**3. Tower of Hanoi, printing the moves.** State the promise first:
*"`hanoi(n, from, to, via)` prints the moves that transfer the top n disks from
`from` to `to`."* Then the body is three lines. Count the moves and confirm
2ⁿ − 1.

**4. Naive against memoised Fibonacci.** Time `fib(40)` both ways. Then count
the calls the naive version makes — add a static counter — and compare with
`fib(41)`. The ratio is φ ≈ 1.618.

**5. Break the stack on purpose.** Recurse over a 10⁶-long linked list, observe
the `StackOverflowError`, then fix it twice: with a loop, and by running the
same recursion on a `Thread` with a 256 MB stack. Say which you would ship.

**6. Maximum subarray by halves.** Write the O(n log n) divide and conquer with
the crossing sum, then compare with Kadane's O(n). The point is not that it is
faster — it is not — but that the crossing term is the whole technique.
units.next_up:
Merge sort is the first algorithm here you could not write without trusting a
recursive call. The next unit asks what sorting costs, what it buys — and which
two recursive ideas are worth more than the library call.

invariant.statement: **The promise**: for every input smaller than the current one, `solve` already returns the right answer. That sentence is the recursion's invariant, and it is induction wearing a function signature.
invariant.established: The base case establishes it: the smallest inputs are answered directly, with no call at all, so the promise holds for them without any assumption.
invariant.maintained: The recursive case maintains it. Assume the promise for every strictly smaller input; the body calls only on smaller inputs and combines their answers correctly, so the promise now holds for this input too. The load-bearing word is **strictly** — a call on an input that is not smaller (`solve(n)` inside `solve(n)`, or `mid` that fails to shrink the range) breaks the chain, and the symptom is a `StackOverflowError`.
invariant.at_exit: The top-level call is just one more input of the size you care about. The promise holds for it, so its return value is the answer.
invariant.note: This is why you should never trace a recursion to convince yourself it works: the trace checks one input, and the induction checks all of them. Trace only to find a bug — usually in the base case or the combine.

variants.name: Linear (decrement)
variants.change: One call on `n − 1` (or the tail of a list), then an O(1) combine.
variants.when: Sums, list walks, counting down. Mostly a teaching shape — a loop is better.
variants.gotcha: The stack is the cost. At n = 10⁵ a Java recursion like this overflows; the loop version does not.

variants.name: Halving
variants.change: One call on `n / 2`, and the result is reused.
variants.when: Fast power, binary search written recursively, `kth-symbol-grammar`.
variants.gotcha: Store the half in a local. Two calls turns log n into n.

variants.name: Binary branching, overlapping
variants.change: Two calls on `n − 1` and `n − 2` (or similar) whose sub-arguments collide.
variants.when: Fibonacci, binomial coefficients, grid paths.
variants.cost: O(2ⁿ) naive → O(n) or O(n²) memoised
variants.gotcha: The exponential is waste, not work. Add a memo keyed by the arguments.

variants.name: Binary branching, output-sized
variants.change: Two calls whose results are genuinely different and all needed.
variants.when: Tower of Hanoi, Gray code, generating subsets.
variants.cost: O(2ⁿ) — and that is the size of the answer
variants.gotcha: No memo can help: the output itself is exponential. Say so rather than trying to optimise it.

variants.name: Divide and conquer
variants.change: Split into independent halves, solve both, and combine with a linear pass across the midpoint.
variants.when: Merge sort, counting inversions, maximum subarray by halves, closest pair.
variants.cost: O(n log n) when the combine is O(n)
variants.gotcha: The halves must be **independent**. If they share subproblems, it is DP.

variants.name: Return a list of results
variants.change: Each call returns *all* answers for its piece; the combine takes a product.
variants.when: Ways to add parentheses, unique BSTs, expression trees.
variants.gotcha: Memoise on the substring or range when pieces repeat — they usually do.

variants.name: Accumulator passed down
variants.change: Carry the partial answer as a parameter instead of combining on the way up.
variants.when: Path sums, building a string, tail-recursive loops.
variants.cost: Same time; the combine moves into the argument
variants.gotcha: A mutable accumulator shared between branches must be undone after each call — that is backtracking.

rewrites.title: Fibonacci, from exponential to linear
rewrites.edit: Two lines: look the argument up before recursing, and store the result before returning.
rewrites.why:
The call tree of naive `fib(n)` has about φⁿ nodes, but only **n distinct
arguments**. Every node beyond the first for each argument is the same question
asked again.

The memo makes the second asking free. Each argument is now computed once, at
O(1) work beyond its two lookups, so the whole tree collapses to n nodes.

**No answer is lost** because `fib(k)` depends on nothing but `k` — a pure
function — so a stored result is the result. That condition is exactly what
fails when a recursion reads or mutates shared state, and why memoising a
backtracking search is usually wrong.

rewrites.title: Fast power: one call, not two
rewrites.edit: The repeated call becomes a local variable.
rewrites.why:
Each level of the slow version makes two calls on half the exponent, so the
recurrence is `T(e) = 2T(e/2) + O(1)` — which is O(e), exactly the cost of
multiplying in a loop. The halving bought nothing.

Storing the result makes it `T(e) = T(e/2) + O(1)` = O(log e). It is the same
insight as memoisation, at its smallest: the two calls had the **same
argument**, so their results are equal, so one of them is waste.

rewrites.title: A deep recursion, made iterative
rewrites.edit: The call stack becomes a loop variable, because each frame only waits to add 1.
rewrites.why:
Linear recursion stores one frame per element, so its **space** is O(n) even
though it allocates nothing. The JVM's default thread stack holds roughly
10,000–20,000 small frames; a 10⁵-node list throws `StackOverflowError`.

The recursive version does nothing after its call except `1 +`. Whenever the
work after the call is that simple, the frame can be replaced by an accumulator
and the recursion by a loop. Java does not do this for you (there is no
tail-call elimination), so you do it by hand.

When the work after the call is *not* simple — a tree with two children, a
DFS — the rewrite needs an explicit `Deque` as the stack instead.

quizzes.prompt: `sort(a, 0, n)` never returns on any array with at least one element. Which change fixes it?
quizzes.answer: The base case must be `hi - lo < 2`
options: The base case must be `hi - lo < 2`
The second call must be `sort(a, mid + 1, hi)`
`merge` must run before the two recursive calls
quizzes.why:
With one element, `hi = lo + 1`, so `mid = lo`. The first call gets the empty range
`[lo, lo)` and returns, but the second call is `sort(a, lo, hi)` — **the same range
again**. The recursion never shrinks. A one-element range is already sorted, so it
has to be a base case: stop at `hi - lo < 2`.

`mid + 1` looks like a fix but skips element `mid` entirely in a half-open range.

quizzes.prompt: `ways(9999)` is correct but never finishes. Why?
quizzes.answer: 0 is a real answer (every odd n), so those states are never treated as cached
options: 0 is a real answer (every odd n), so those states are never treated as cached
The memo array is too small for n = 9999
quizzes.why:
4s and 6s only make even numbers, so `ways(n) = 0` for every odd n — and `0` is also
the "not computed yet" marker. Every odd state looks uncached forever, and the call
tree for an odd argument stays exponential.

Use a separate marker that cannot be an answer: fill the memo with `-1`, or keep a
`boolean[] done`.

quizzes.prompt: What does `f(4071)` print?
quizzes.why:
The print runs **before** the call, on the way down, so digits come out last-first:
1, 7, 0, 4. Move the print below the call and the same digits come out on the way
back up, in order — `4071`. That one line's position is the whole of
`to-base-recursive`.

quizzes.prompt: How many calls does the naive `fib(5)` make in total, counting the first?
quizzes.why:
Let C(n) be the number of calls: C(0) = C(1) = 1 and C(n) = 1 + C(n − 1) + C(n − 2).
So C(2) = 3, C(3) = 5, C(4) = 9, C(5) = 15. The count grows like Fibonacci itself —
about 1.6ⁿ — while only six distinct arguments ever appear. That gap is what a memo
removes.

quizzes.prompt: The moves this prints are illegal — a larger disk lands on a smaller one. Which change fixes it?
quizzes.answer: The first call must be `hanoi(n - 1, from, via, to)`
options: The first call must be `hanoi(n - 1, from, via, to)`
The second call must be `hanoi(n - 1, via, from, to)`
The print must come before the first call
quizzes.why:
State the promise: *`hanoi(k, from, to, via)` moves the top k disks from `from` to
`to`*. To move disk n, the n − 1 disks above it must first go **out of the way** —
to `via` — so the first call's target is `via`, using `to` as the spare. As written
it stacks them on `to`, exactly where disk n is about to go.

quizzes.prompt: Merge sort on n = 1,000,000 elements, recursing on halves. Roughly how deep does the call stack get?
quizzes.answer: About 20 frames
quizzes.why:
Each level halves the range, so the depth is ⌈log₂ 10⁶⌉ ≈ 20 — and the two calls at
a level run one *after* the other, so they never stack. Merge sort's recursion is
harmless; a recursion that shrinks by **one** per call (a list walk, Josephus) is
the kind that reaches 10⁶ frames and overflows.

stuck.when: I do not know what the function should return
stuck.ask: Write its promise as one sentence: *for any input of this shape, it returns …*. If you cannot finish the sentence, the parameters are wrong — you usually need one more (an index, a bound, a partial result).

stuck.when: I cannot find the base case
stuck.ask: What is the smallest input whose answer is obvious — 0, empty, one element, a leaf? Then check the combine step works when the sub-answer *is* that base value.

stuck.when: I do not see how to make the problem smaller
stuck.ask: Try the three standard cuts: remove one element (first or last), halve it, or split at every possible point. Keep whichever leaves a problem of the **same shape**.

stuck.when: I keep tracing the calls and losing my place
stuck.ask: Stop tracing. Assume the smaller call already returns the right answer and write only what you do with it. Trace only to debug one failing input, two levels deep.

stuck.when: It is correct but far too slow
stuck.ask: Print the arguments on entry. The same arguments twice means memoise. A depth close to n with n near 10⁵ means rewrite it as a loop.

stuck.when: I can solve each half but not the whole (divide and conquer)
stuck.ask: List the three places the answer can be: left half, right half, straddling the middle. The straddling case is the only new code — write it on its own.

edge_cases.breaks: A base case written as `e == 1`, or one that returns the base instead of 1.
The odd branch — `half * half * b` with `half = power(b, 0) = 1`.
A base case that only handles `n == 1`, recursing into negative n.
A base case of `hi - lo < 1`, which recurses forever on one element.
A merge that forgets to copy the leftover tail of one half.
The recursive recurrence — it needs 10⁶ stack frames and throws `StackOverflowError`.
A base case of `x == 0 → ""`, which prints nothing for zero.
A strip test using `<=`, or a combine that forgets distance 0 is possible.

walkthrough.title: Last One Standing — from simulation to a one-line recurrence

steps.name: Read
steps.body:
*n people in a circle; count k, the k-th leaves; repeat; who survives?* Constraints:
n ≤ 10⁶, k ≤ 10⁹. Output one number. The answer depends only on n and k — no array
of data at all, which is the first hint that the answer has a formula-like
structure.

steps.name: Route
steps.body:
"The answer for n in terms of the answer for n − 1" is the recursion signal. After
one removal the circle is a smaller instance of the same problem — only the
numbering has shifted. That is exactly the shape the recursion unit teaches:
*same problem, smaller input*.

steps.name: Brute force
steps.body:
Simulate: keep a list, remove index `(i + k − 1) % size`, repeat. Each removal from
an `ArrayList` is O(n), so the whole thing is O(n²) — 10¹² at n = 10⁶. Too slow, but
worth writing: it is the oracle you will test the fast version against.

steps.name: Insight
steps.body:
Number positions from 0. The first to leave is at `(k − 1) mod n`; counting resumes
at `k mod n`. Relabel that person as 0 and you have a circle of n − 1 people whose
survivor is J(n − 1) **in the new numbering**. Shifting back adds k:

```
J(1) = 0
J(n) = (J(n − 1) + k) mod n
```

The recursion is correct and 10⁶ frames deep, which Java's stack will not hold. The
work happens after the call, so the loop that computes J(1), J(2), … in order is
the same computation, bottom-up.

steps.name: Code
Test and price
steps.body:
- `1 5` → 1 (one person). `6 2` → 5 (check against the simulation by hand).
- `5 1000000000` — k far larger than n; the `% m` handles it, and `long` keeps
  `pos + k` safe.
- `1000000 2` — the case the recursive version dies on.

**Cost:** O(n) time, O(1) space. Diff it against the simulation for every n ≤ 50 and
k ≤ 10 before trusting it.

units.title: Sorting & Ordering
units.tagline: What sorting costs, what it buys, and the two sorting ideas worth more than the call.
units.why:
You will rarely ship your own sort. You will constantly *decide whether to call
one*, and that decision is one of the most reliable dividing lines between an
O(n²) solution and an O(n log n) one. Sorting by a **derived key** — by
frequency, by the second element, with a tie-break — is the part of that call
interviews test directly, and writing the `Comparator` correctly is a small
skill with a large payoff.

But two sorting *algorithms* are worth knowing from the inside, because their
ideas solve problems no library call does. **Quickselect** is quicksort that
recurses into one side only, and finds the k-th element in O(n) average. **Merge
sort's merge** sees every pair that crosses the midpoint, so it can *count*
them — inversions, smaller-to-the-right, pairs with a condition — in O(n log n).
units.model:
### What a sort costs

`Arrays.sort` on primitives is a dual-pivot quicksort: O(n log n) average, no
extra memory, **not stable**. On objects it is Timsort: O(n log n) worst case,
O(n) extra memory, and **stable** — equal elements keep their relative order.
That difference matters when you sort twice to get a tie-break.

### What it buys

| After sorting | You can |
| --- | --- |
| Duplicates are adjacent | Detect them in one pass |
| Extremes are at the ends | Answer k-th smallest/largest by index |
| Order is monotone | Binary search |
| Intervals share a start order | Merge and sweep them |
| Pairs are directional | Converge two pointers |

### Sorting by a key

```java
Integer[] a = ...;                         // objects, not int[]
Arrays.sort(a, (x, y) -> freq.get(x) - freq.get(y));   // ← subtraction: risky
Arrays.sort(a, Comparator.comparingInt(freq::get));    // ← safe
```

Never subtract inside a comparator unless the values are provably small:
`Integer.MIN_VALUE - 1` overflows and reverses the sign, which corrupts the
sort silently. `Comparator.comparingInt` and `Integer.compare` are safe.

Descending, and with a tie-break:

```java
Arrays.sort(a, Comparator
    .comparingInt(freq::get).reversed()
    .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
```

A comparator must be **consistent**: if `c(x, y) < 0` then `c(y, x) > 0`, and
the relation must be transitive. An inconsistent comparator does not merely
produce a wrong order — Java detects some cases and throws.

### When not to sort

If the values are small integers, counting sort is O(n) and beats it: the
O(n log n) lower bound only binds sorts that learn from comparisons, and using a
value as an array index learns more. If you only need the k largest, a heap is
O(n log k). If you only need the k-th, quickselect is O(n) average. Sorting is
the general answer, not always the best one — and saying so is worth points.

### Quickselect

Partition around a pivot the way quicksort does, so everything smaller is on
the left and everything larger on the right. The pivot is now at its final
sorted index p. If p is the index you want, stop; otherwise recurse into **one**
side only.

```java
int select(int[] a, int lo, int hi, int k) {        // k-th smallest, 0-based, in [lo, hi]
    while (true) {
        int p = partition(a, lo, hi);                 // random pivot → its sorted index
        if (p == k) return a[p];
        if (p < k) lo = p + 1; else hi = p - 1;       // discard the other side
    }
}
```

Each round discards a constant fraction on average, so the work is
n + n/2 + n/4 + … = O(n). A pivot that is always the smallest element makes it
O(n²) — which is why the pivot is **random**.

### Merge sort, reused

The recursion unit's merge takes elements from two sorted halves. When it takes
from the **right** half while `mid − i` elements are still waiting in the left,
each of those is larger and comes earlier: `mid − i` inversions, counted in O(1).

```java
while (i < mid && j < hi) {
    if (a[i] <= a[j]) buf[k++] = a[i++];
    else { inversions += mid - i; buf[k++] = a[j++]; }
}
```

Every cross-midpoint pair is seen exactly once across the recursion, so the
count costs nothing beyond the sort itself.
units.internals:
### What `Arrays.sort` actually runs

| Call | Algorithm | Stable | Worst case | Extra memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Arrays.sort(int[])` (and every primitive) | Dual-pivot quicksort | No | O(n log n)* | O(log n) |
| `Arrays.sort(T[])`, `List.sort`, `Collections.sort` | Timsort | **Yes** | O(n log n) | O(n) |
| `Arrays.parallelSort` | Parallel merge + the above | Primitives: no | O(n log n) | O(n) |

*Modern JDKs fall back to heapsort when the quicksort recursion gets too deep,
so adversarial inputs no longer degrade primitives to O(n²).

**Why primitives may be unstable.** Stability means equal elements keep their
input order — but two equal `int`s are indistinguishable, so there is nothing to
preserve. Objects carry identity and other fields, so their sort must be stable,
and Timsort is.

### Insertion sort, hiding inside both

Below a small cutoff (tens of elements), both algorithms switch to insertion
sort. It is O(n²) but has almost no overhead and runs in cache, so on 30
elements it beats everything asymptotically better. That is also why "sort
the small subproblem with insertion sort" is a standard optimisation of your own
merge sort.

### Timsort in one paragraph

Real data is rarely random: it has **runs** — stretches already ascending or
descending. Timsort finds them, reverses the descending ones, extends short ones
with insertion sort, and merges runs from a stack under balance rules. On sorted
or nearly sorted input it is O(n). When one run keeps winning during a merge it
**gallops** — exponential then binary search — to copy a block at once.

### The Ω(n log n) lower bound

A comparison sort learns one bit per comparison. There are n! possible input
orders and it must distinguish all of them, so it needs at least log₂(n!)
comparisons, and log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n − 1.44n. **No comparison sort can beat
O(n log n).**

Counting sort and radix sort are not comparison sorts: indexing an array by a
value extracts many bits at once. That is how they reach O(n + k) — and why they
need a bounded key.

### Why the comparator contract matters

Timsort's merge assumes transitivity. When your comparator violates it
(`compare(a, b) < 0`, `compare(b, c) < 0` but `compare(a, c) > 0`), Timsort can
detect a contradiction mid-merge and throw `IllegalArgumentException:
Comparison method violates its general contract!` — typically only on larger
inputs, where the galloping path is taken. A comparator using `>=` for "less
than", or comparing doubles containing NaN, is the usual cause.

signals.reach_for: Sort, or a heap, or quickselect
signals.why: Sorting is O(n log n); a size-k heap is O(n log k); quickselect O(n) average.

signals.reach_for: Count, then sort by the count
signals.why: Two phases: build the map, then order its entries.
Or hash them — hashing is O(n) and sorting is O(n log n).

signals.when: Values are small integers or letters
signals.why: O(n + k) beats O(n log n) when k is bounded.
Ordering is the precondition for every interval sweep.

signals.when: Ties must break a particular way
signals.why: Chain, never nest `if`s.

skeletons.name: Sort and scan
skeletons.when: Duplicates, closest pair, k-th by index.
skeletons.note: Sortedness makes “equal” mean “adjacent”.

skeletons.name: Sort by a derived key
skeletons.when: By frequency, by a field, by a computed score.
skeletons.note: `comparingInt` instead of a subtraction; `thenComparing` for the tie-break.

skeletons.name: Counting sort
skeletons.when: Small bounded values — O(n), not O(n log n).
skeletons.note: Only viable when the value range is comparable to n.

skeletons.name: Quickselect
skeletons.when: The k-th smallest or largest, without sorting everything.
skeletons.note: k-th largest is `kthSmallest(a, n − k)`. The random pivot is what makes O(n) the expected case.

skeletons.name: Count while merging
skeletons.when: Inversions, and any "pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]" count.
skeletons.note: `<=`, not `<`: equal values are not an inversion. The count can reach n²/2 — use `long`.

skeletons.name: Three-way partition
skeletons.when: Many duplicates; sort-colours; quicksort that survives equal keys.
skeletons.note: Four regions, and the unexamined one is `[i, gt]`. Write them above the loop.

skeletons.name: LSD radix sort (non-negative ints)
skeletons.when: Fixed-width keys — O(4 · (n + 256)) with no comparisons.
skeletons.note: Four stable counting passes, one byte each. Stability is what lets later passes keep earlier ones' work.

traces.title: Insertion sort: [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3]
traces.intro: The prefix `a[0..i−1]` is always sorted. Take `a[i]`, shift every larger element in the prefix one place right, and drop it into the gap.
traces.takeaway: Nine shifts in total, and that number is exactly the count of *inversions* — pairs that are out of order. That is why insertion sort is O(n²) on reversed input and O(n) on nearly-sorted input, and why TimSort uses it for short runs.

traces.title: Lomuto partition of [7, 2, 9, 4, 1, 8, 5] around the last element, 5
traces.intro: `p` is the boundary: `a[0..p)` holds everything found so far that is < 5. `i` scans left to right; a small element is swapped to the boundary and the boundary moves.
traces.takeaway: The pivot lands at index 3 and never moves again: three smaller values to its left, three larger to its right, neither side sorted. Quickselect asking for index 3 stops here; asking for index 5 throws away `2 4 1 5` and partitions only `9 8 7`.

traces.title: Three-way partition of [4, 9, 4, 1, 7, 4, 2] around 4
traces.intro: Four regions: `[0, lt)` < 4, `[lt, i)` = 4, `[i, gt]` unexamined, `(gt, end]` > 4. The loop ends when the unexamined region is empty.
rows: 2 < 4: swap into the < region, lt++ i++
1 < 4: swap into the < region, lt++ i++
traces.takeaway: All three 4s end up together in the middle, `[lt, i)`, and quicksort never touches them again. Watch the rows where a large value is swapped in from `gt`: `i` does not move, because the value that arrives there has not been looked at.

traces.title: LSD radix sort, base 10: [512, 38, 207, 91, 450, 26, 873]
traces.intro: Three stable passes, least significant digit first. Each pass looks at one digit only, and keeps equal digits in the order the previous pass left them.
traces.takeaway: After the tens pass, the last two digits read 07, 12, 26, 38, 50, 73, 91 — in order. The hundreds pass then moves 026, 038 and 091 (all hundreds digit 0) to the front and, being stable, keeps them in exactly that order. An unstable pass could emit 091 before 026 and undo both earlier passes. Three passes of O(n + 10), and not one comparison between two numbers.

costs.note: Better than sorting when k ≪ n.
The count rides along with the merge.

pitfalls.symptom: The sorted order is subtly wrong on extreme values
pitfalls.cause: A comparator written as `a - b`, which overflows when the values are far apart.
pitfalls.fix: `Integer.compare(a, b)` or `Comparator.comparingInt(...)`.

pitfalls.symptom: “Comparison method violates its general contract!”
pitfalls.cause: The comparator is inconsistent — often a `>=` where `>` was meant, or NaN in a double comparison.
pitfalls.fix: Make it antisymmetric and transitive; prefer the `Comparator` factories.

pitfalls.symptom: Sorting destroys the answer
pitfalls.cause: The problem asks for original indices, which sorting moves.
pitfalls.fix: Sort index pairs, or use hashing instead.

pitfalls.symptom: `Arrays.sort` on `int[]` is not stable and the tie-break is lost
pitfalls.cause: Primitive sorts give no stability guarantee.
pitfalls.fix: Box to `Integer[]` and sort with a comparator when order among equals matters.

pitfalls.symptom: Sorting to find one element
pitfalls.cause: O(n log n) spent where a single O(n) pass — or a size-k heap — would do.
pitfalls.fix: Ask what you actually need: the max, the top k, or the whole order.

pitfalls.symptom: Quickselect times out on sorted input
pitfalls.cause: The pivot is always the first or last element, so each partition removes one element and the total is O(n²).
pitfalls.fix: Pick the pivot at random (or shuffle once first).

pitfalls.symptom: The inversion count is too high on inputs with duplicates
pitfalls.cause: The merge takes from the right half when values are equal, counting equal pairs.
pitfalls.fix: Take from the left on ties: `a[i] <= a[j]`.

pitfalls.symptom: Radix sort output is sorted by the last digit only
pitfalls.cause: A pass was not stable — it wrote buckets front to back from the wrong end, or sorted in place.
pitfalls.fix: Prefix-sum the counts and fill the output **from the back**, walking the input backwards.

pitfalls.symptom: Three-way partition skips elements or loops forever
pitfalls.cause: `i` advanced after swapping with `gt`, or the loop ran `i < gt` with an inclusive `gt`.
pitfalls.fix: Decide whether `gt` is inclusive, write the four regions down, and advance `i` only on the `<` and `=` branches.

pitfalls.symptom: Sorting a huge `Integer[]` is far slower than expected
pitfalls.cause: Boxed comparisons and a lambda call per comparison, on top of Timsort's O(n) buffer.
pitfalls.fix: Sort a primitive array where possible — pack `(key, index)` into a `long`.

checks.q: Why is `(a, b) -> a - b` a dangerous comparator?
checks.a: The subtraction can overflow `int` for far-apart values and flip its sign, silently corrupting the order. `Integer.compare` cannot.

checks.q: When does counting sort beat a comparison sort?
checks.a: When the value range k is O(n) or smaller — it is O(n + k), and comparison sorts cannot beat O(n log n) in general.

checks.q: You need only the 5 largest of 10⁶ values. Sort?
checks.a: No. A size-5 min-heap is O(n log k) ≈ O(n), and uses O(k) memory instead of ordering the whole array.

checks.q: What does stability mean, and when do you need it?
checks.a: Equal elements keep their input order. You need it when you sort by one key and rely on a previous sort to break ties.

checks.q: Why is quickselect O(n) on average when quicksort is O(n log n)?
checks.a: After partitioning, quickselect recurses into one side only. The sizes shrink geometrically — n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n — instead of every level processing all n.

checks.q: During merge sort's merge, a[j] from the right half is taken while i < mid. How many inversions does that reveal?
checks.a: `mid − i`: every element still waiting in the left half is larger than a[j] and sits before it in the original array.

checks.q: Why can no comparison sort beat O(n log n)?
checks.a: Each comparison yields one bit, and the sort must tell apart all n! input orders, so it needs at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n comparisons.

checks.q: Radix sort processes the least significant digit first. What property must each pass have, and why?
checks.a: Stability. After sorting by digit d, elements equal in d must keep the order the earlier (less significant) passes gave them — otherwise that work is lost.

checks.q: In a three-way partition, why does the `> pivot` branch not advance `i`?
checks.a: It swaps `a[i]` with `a[gt]`, bringing in an element nobody has examined. Advancing `i` would skip it.

checks.q: How do you sort by a key but still report original indices?
checks.a: Sort an index array (`Integer[] idx`) with a comparator that reads `a[idx[i]]` — an argsort — or sort `(value, index)` pairs.

checks.q: Why does `largest-number` need a pairwise comparator rather than a key?
checks.a: Whether x goes before y depends on y: compare the concatenations `x + y` and `y + x`. There is no single number per element that captures that.

bigo.code:
List<Integer> xs = new ArrayList<>(input);   // n values
Collections.sort(xs);
bigo.why: `Collections.sort` is TimSort: O(n log n) worst case, and O(n) on input that is already sorted — it finds existing runs and merges them.

bigo.code: words.sort((a, b) -> a.toLowerCase().compareTo(b.toLowerCase()));  // n words of length k
bigo.why: A sort makes O(n log n) comparisons, and this comparator allocates two lowercase copies each time, so every comparison is O(k). Precompute the keys once — or use `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER`, which compares in place.

Insertion sort is O(n + inversions). Nearly-sorted input has almost no inversions, so the inner loop does O(1) work per element. Its worst case is O(n²), which is why it is only chosen when the input is known to be close.

Counting sort never compares, so the n log n lower bound does not apply. The `while` writes each element once in total, plus one visit per value in the range. Wonderful when K is small; useless when K is 10⁹.
A running median by re-sorting everything seen so far: the i-th step costs O(i log i), which sums to O(n² log n). Two heaps maintain the median in O(log n) per element, O(n log n) overall.
On sorted input the last element is the maximum, so each partition places it at `hi` and removes only one element: n + (n−1) + … = O(n²). A random pivot restores the O(n) expectation.
Four passes, each O(n + 256). The number of passes depends on the key *width*, not on n, so it is O(n) — which is how radix sort sidesteps the n log n bound: it never compares two elements.

No element is `< pivot`, so the pivot always lands at `lo` and the right side has n − 1 elements. Duplicates degrade a two-way partition to the sorted-input worst case; a three-way partition puts every equal value in the middle and finishes in one O(n) pass.

units.interview:
The sorting question in an interview is usually "you sorted; did you need to?".
Have the three alternatives ready: counting sort when the range is small, a heap
when you want the top k, quickselect when you want exactly the k-th — and be
able to *write* quickselect, because "the k-th largest in O(n)" is a common
follow-up. When a problem asks to count pairs that are out of order, say
"merge sort, counting at the merge" before anything else.

### Say it out loud

- *"Do I need the whole order? If only the k-th, quickselect is O(n) average."*
- *"I'll use `Integer.compare`, not subtraction — subtraction overflows."*
- *"`Arrays.sort` on primitives isn't stable; I need stability here, so I'll sort
  objects (or pack the key and index into a long)."*
- *"Counting out-of-order pairs: merge sort, adding `mid − i` when the right side
  wins."*

rungs.title: Warm up
rungs.purpose: Order by something other than the value itself.

notes.sort-by-frequency: Count first, then sort the keys by their count with a tie-break. The comparator is the whole exercise.
notes.counting-sort-ages: No comparisons at all: the value is the index. O(n + k) because k = 151.
notes.rank-transform: Sort a copy, dedupe, binary-search each original value. Compare with leaderboard-ranks: dense ranks versus competition ranks.

rungs.title: Core
rungs.purpose: Sort by a rule, then read the answer off the order.

notes.largest-number: No sort key exists, so compare pairs: x before y when x+y beats y+x.

rungs.title: Quickselect
rungs.purpose: The k-th element in O(n) average — partition once, recurse into one side only.

notes.kth-largest-element: Solve it by sorting first, then with quickselect: partition around a random pivot and recurse into the side that holds index n − k.
notes.moves-to-median: Prove the median is optimal first (moving the target up helps while more values are above it). Then find it with quickselect.

rungs.title: Non-comparison sorts
rungs.purpose: Sorting without comparing: the value, or one digit of it, is the index.

notes.radix-pass-by-pass: Each pass is a stable counting sort on one digit. Print after every pass and check the invariant: sorted by the last p digits.

rungs.title: Merge sort, reused
rungs.purpose: The merge step sees every pair that crosses the midpoint — so it can count them.

notes.count-inversions: Merge sort from the recursion unit. When the right half's element is taken first, it jumps every remaining element of the left half: add `mid − i`.
notes.important-reverse-pairs: Count in a separate two-pointer pass before merging — the merge compares a[i] with a[j], not with 2·a[j]. And 2·a[j] needs a long.

rungs.title: Extra practice
rungs.purpose: More orderings — optional, counted only once started.

notes.maximum-gap: Pigeonhole: buckets narrower than the average gap mean the answer lies between buckets.
notes.sort-by-bits: Two keys in one comparator — or packed into a single int key.
notes.first-missing-positive: Cyclic sort: every value in 1..n has a home index, so the array is its own hash set.
notes.relative-sort-array: Small values: a counting array replaces the comparator.
notes.height-checker: Counting sort over a tiny value range replays the expected order.
notes.best-meeting-point-line: The median, not the mean. Step the meeting point by one and watch the total change.
notes.kth-smallest: The same partition, a different target index. A random pivot is what keeps the worst case away.
notes.leaderboard-ranks: Two keys, one descending, and ranks that are shared on ties and then skip. Write the comparator with `Integer.compare`.
notes.custom-sort-string: A custom order is a rank; with 26 letters, count instead of compare.
notes.h-index: Sorted descending, a paper's rank counts the papers at least as good. Then cap at n and count.
notes.count-range-sums: Subarrays are pairs of prefix sums. Merge-count them, with a *window* of valid partners per left element instead of a single pointer.

units.build_it:
### Five sorts and a test harness

**0. The harness first.** Write `check(int[] a)`: clone, sort with your
implementation, and compare with `Arrays.sort`. Run it on 1,000 random arrays of
random length 0–50 with values in a small range (lots of duplicates) and a large
one. Every step below uses it.

**1. Insertion sort.** Shift, do not swap. Then count the shifts, and notice the
count is exactly the number of inversions — insertion sort is an inversion
counter running in O(n + inversions).

**2. Merge sort** with one buffer, then the inversion counter from the rewrites
above. Test the count against the O(n²) double loop.

**3. Quicksort with a three-way partition.** `lt`, `i`, `gt`: `< pivot` goes left
and both advance; `> pivot` swaps with `gt` and **only `gt` moves**; equal just
advances `i`. Write the invariant for all four regions before coding. Then feed
it an array of 10⁵ equal values and confirm it is not O(n²).

**4. Quickselect** on top of the same partition. Test the k-th against the
sorted array for every k.

**5. LSD radix sort** on non-negative ints, base 256, four passes, each a stable
counting sort into a buffer. Then extend it to negative values (flip the sign
bit before bucketing) and run the harness.

**6. A comparator contract tester.** Given `Comparator<T>` and a list, check
antisymmetry (`sgn(c(a,b)) == -sgn(c(b,a))`) and transitivity on all triples.
Run it on `(a, b) -> a - b` over values near `Integer.MIN_VALUE` and watch it fail.
units.next_up:
