intervals that end before it starts — and since the ends are **sorted**, that
predecessor is one binary search away:

```java
// iv sorted by end; ends[i] = iv[i].end
best[0] = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    int[] cur = iv[i - 1];
    int j = upperBound(ends, cur.start);          // # intervals ending <= start
    best[i] = Math.max(best[i - 1], best[j] + cur.weight);
}
```

O(n log n), and every piece of it is from this stage: the sort, the binary
search, and the recognition that a local rule has stopped being safe.

### Total covered length, and subtraction

Two more questions reduce to merging. The **length of the union** is the sum of
the merged blocks' lengths — merge, then add. **Removing** a range `[x, y)`
from a sorted list is the insert-interval three phases with one change: an
overlapping interval is *trimmed* to the part outside `[x, y)`, which can leave
zero, one or two pieces.

signals.why: Build left to right, extending with `max`.
Earliest finish leaves the most room.

signals.reach_for: Sweep or a min-heap of end times
signals.why: The answer is the peak concurrency.

signals.when: “insert into a sorted list of intervals”
signals.why: Everything before, the merged block, everything after.
Advance whichever ends first.

signals.reach_for: Merge everything, then read the gaps
signals.why: The complement of the merged set.

skeletons.name: Merge overlapping
skeletons.when: The base operation almost everything else builds on.
skeletons.note: `max` on the end — the new interval may be nested inside the last.

skeletons.name: Insert one interval
skeletons.when: Into an already-sorted, non-overlapping list.
skeletons.note: Three loops, each with a clear job. Do not try to fuse them.

skeletons.name: Peak concurrency (heap)
skeletons.when: Minimum meeting rooms, maximum simultaneous anything.
skeletons.note: The heap size is the number of rooms in use; its peak is the answer. Only `offer`, `peek` and `poll` are needed here — the heaps unit (stage 5) explains why each is cheap.

skeletons.name: Intersect two sorted lists
skeletons.when: Overlap of two schedules.
skeletons.note: Advancing the earlier end is what makes the single pass sufficient.

traces.title: Merging intervals: [8, 10], [1, 3], [15, 18], [2, 6], [9, 12]
traces.intro: After sorting by start, an interval can only overlap the *last* merged interval, so one comparison per interval is enough.
rows: no overlap — start a new interval
no overlap — start a new interval
no overlap — start a new interval
traces.takeaway: Five intervals become three: [1, 6], [8, 12], [15, 18]. The `max` on the end matters — an interval swallowed entirely by the previous one (like [2, 4] inside [1, 6]) must not *shrink* the end. Without the sort, [1, 3] and [2, 6] are two positions apart and a single pass would miss them.

traces.title: Insert [4, 9] into [1,2] [3,5] [6,7] [8,10] [12,16]
traces.intro: The list is already sorted and disjoint, so it splits into three runs: entirely before the new interval, touching it, entirely after. One loop each.
rows: starts after the new end: copy
traces.takeaway: Three intervals collapse into [3, 10] — `min` on the start (3 < 4) and `max` on the end (10 > 9). Every interval is read once and nothing is sorted: O(n). Written as a single loop with flags, this is where people lose an hour.

traces.title: Minimum rooms by a ±1 sweep: [1,4) [2,6) [3,7) [4,8) [6,9) [7,10)
traces.intro: Twelve events sorted by time; at equal times the −1 sorts first (−1 < +1), so a room freed at 4 is reusable by a meeting starting at 4.
traces.takeaway: Three rooms suffice. Now flip the tie rule: at time 4, [4,8) would be counted before [1,4) is released, the count would briefly read 4, and the answer would claim four rooms for a schedule that fits in three. Every peak-concurrency bug with back-to-back bookings is that one tie.

traces.title: Weighted interval scheduling, sorted by end
traces.intro: `best[i]` is the most weight using only the first i intervals. `p` counts the intervals ending at or before this one's start — one binary search over the sorted ends — and they are exactly the ones compatible with taking it.
traces.takeaway: The answer is 15: [2,10) alone. Greedy by end time keeps [1,4), [5,8) and [9,12) — three intervals, the most of any selection, but worth only 13. Maximising the *count* and maximising the *weight* are different problems. The sort and the binary search are the same as always; only the choice became a `max`.

costs.note: No sort needed — it is already ordered.

pitfalls.symptom: Maximum non-overlapping selection is too small
pitfalls.cause: The intervals were sorted by start time.
pitfalls.fix: Sort by end. This is the single most common interval mistake.

pitfalls.symptom: A merged interval is shorter than one it contains
pitfalls.cause: The end was overwritten rather than maximised.
pitfalls.fix: `last[1] = Math.max(last[1], cur[1])` — nested intervals are real.

pitfalls.symptom: One room too many
pitfalls.cause: A start was processed before an end at the same timestamp.
pitfalls.fix: Release first: use `ends[j] <= starts[i]` in the sweep.

pitfalls.symptom: Touching intervals are treated inconsistently
pitfalls.cause: `[1,2]` and `[2,3]` were merged in one place and separated in another.
pitfalls.fix: Decide from the statement whether contact counts, and use the same comparison everywhere.

pitfalls.symptom: Sorting an already-sorted input
pitfalls.cause: An extra O(n log n) where the list was given in order.
pitfalls.fix: Insert-into-sorted is O(n); check what the input guarantees.

pitfalls.symptom: The sort comparator overflows
pitfalls.cause: `(a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]` with coordinates near `Integer.MAX_VALUE`.
pitfalls.fix: `Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])`.

pitfalls.symptom: Weighted scheduling answer is too small
pitfalls.cause: The greedy by end time was used, or the predecessor search excluded intervals that end exactly when the current one starts.
pitfalls.fix: DP over intervals sorted by end, with `upperBound(ends, start)` for the predecessor count.

pitfalls.symptom: Subtracting a range deletes an interval that should have been split
pitfalls.cause: Only the left or the right remainder of an overlapping interval was kept.
pitfalls.fix: An interval overlapping `[x, y)` can leave a piece before x **and** a piece after y. Emit each if it is non-empty.

pitfalls.symptom: The ±1 sweep counts back-to-back meetings as overlapping
pitfalls.cause: Events at the same time were sorted with `+1` before `−1`.
pitfalls.fix: Tie-break by delta ascending so ends (−1) are processed first.

checks.q: Merging wants one sort order and scheduling wants another. Which and why?
checks.a: Merging sorts by **start**, because it builds the result left to right. Maximum non-overlapping scheduling sorts by **end**, because finishing earliest leaves the most room for what follows.

checks.q: Write the overlap test for [a1,a2] and [b1,b2].
checks.a: `a1 <= b2 && b1 <= a2`. Whether the endpoints touching counts as overlap is a specification decision and must be applied consistently.

checks.q: Why must an end event be processed before a start at the same time?
checks.a: Otherwise a resource that is being released at that instant is not yet available, and the peak count is one too high.

checks.q: How do you compute free time across many busy intervals?
checks.a: Merge all the busy intervals, then emit the gaps between consecutive merged blocks.

checks.q: Why is merging linear after the sort — why only compare with the last block?
checks.a: Blocks before the last one ended before the last block began, and every future interval starts at or after the current one. So nothing still to come can reach an earlier block.

checks.q: Maximum total weight of non-overlapping intervals: why does sort-by-end greedy fail, and what replaces it?
checks.a: One heavy interval can beat several light ones that finish earlier. Sort by end and DP: `best[i] = max(best[i−1], w_i + best[p(i)])`, where p(i) is found by binary search over the sorted ends.

checks.q: Minimum arrows to burst balloons: why sort by end and shoot at the end?
checks.a: The balloon ending first must be hit by some arrow at or before its end; shooting exactly at its end hits it and as many later-starting balloons as any position could.

checks.q: How do you check a new booking against a calendar in O(log n)?
checks.a: Keep bookings in a `TreeMap<start, end>`. The new one clashes iff the floor entry ends after the new start, or the ceiling entry starts before the new end.

bigo.why: Merge intervals: sort by start, then one pass comparing with the last merged interval. Once sorted, an interval can only overlap the one just before it, so no backward search is needed.
Checking every pair is the honest answer when you need *every* overlapping pair — the output itself can be n². When you only need "does any overlap?", sort and compare neighbours in O(n log n).
Meeting rooms: the heap holds the end time of every room in use, and each meeting does at most one poll and one offer. Scanning every room for a free one would be O(n·rooms).

Inserting into an already sorted, disjoint list needs no sort: one pass that copies what is left of the new interval, absorbs what overlaps it, and carries the rest. Re-sorting everything would be the O(n log n) way to get the same answer.
Painting every time slot of every interval. A difference array records only the two endpoints — `diff[start]++`, `diff[end]--` — and one prefix-sum pass recovers the counts: O(n + T).
One binary search per interval, on top of the O(n log n) sort. Trying every subset would be O(2ⁿ); the sorted ends are what make the predecessor a search instead of a scan.
The scan can walk back over every earlier interval — for example when all of them overlap the current one. Correct, and quadratic; the ends are sorted, so the scan should be a binary search.
Each booking does two neighbour lookups and at most one insert in a balanced tree holding at most q entries: O(log q) each. Checking every existing booking instead is O(q²).

units.interview:
Interval questions are a gift when you state the sort rule first: *"merging, so
I sort by start"* or *"maximum non-overlapping, so I sort by end — earliest
finish leaves the most room"*. Then raise the endpoint question before the
interviewer does — does a meeting ending at 2 clash with one starting at 2? —
because it is the ambiguity the test cases are built around.

The common follow-up is to add weights. Say "then greedy fails — sort by end,
binary-search each interval's predecessor, and DP" before being asked; it shows
you know where the technique's edge is.

### Say it out loud

- *"Merging, so I sort by start; the end of a merged block is a max, because
  intervals nest."*
- *"Maximum non-overlapping, so I sort by end — the earliest finish leaves the most
  room."*
- *"Does a meeting ending at 2 clash with one starting at 2? I'll assume not
  unless you say otherwise."*
- *"With weights, greedy fails; sort by end, binary-search the predecessor, and
  DP."*

rungs.title: Warm up
rungs.purpose: The overlap test, applied once.

notes.can-attend-meetings: Sort by start and compare neighbours. Decide what touching endpoints mean before you code.
notes.covered-length-union: Merge, then add the blocks. `max` on the end, and remember the last block after the loop.

rungs.title: Core
rungs.purpose: Merging, and the two-pointer intersection.

notes.merge-intervals: The base operation. `Math.max` on the end, because intervals nest.
notes.insert-interval: Three phases. Trying to write it as one loop is how this becomes hard.
notes.interval-intersections: Two pointers: emit `[max start, min end]` when it is non-empty, then advance whichever interval ends first — it can meet nothing else.
notes.subtract-interval: Insert-interval turned inside out: keep [a, min(b, x)) and [max(a, y), b) when non-empty. No sort — the input is already ordered.

rungs.title: Variations
rungs.purpose: Sweeps and end-time greed.

notes.min-meeting-rooms: Solve it twice — a ±1 sweep and a heap of end times — and notice they are the same algorithm.
notes.non-overlapping-remove: Sort by end and keep greedily; the removals are everything you did not keep.
notes.car-pooling: Peak concurrency weighted by passengers: `+num` at pickup, `−num` at drop-off, drop-offs first at equal positions.
notes.min-arrows-balloons: Sort by end and shoot at the first balloon's end; every balloon starting at or before it bursts. Touching counts here — `<=`, not `<`.
notes.busiest-moment: The ±1 sweep, recording the time whenever the count sets a new record. Pack (time, type) into one long so ends sort first.
notes.covered-by-two: The sweep again, measuring the gaps where the count is at least 2. Change the threshold and the same loop gives the union or the intersection.

rungs.title: Stretch
rungs.purpose: Merge first, then read the complement.

notes.employee-free-time: Flatten every schedule, merge, and emit the gaps. A heap-based k-way merge avoids sorting everything.

rungs.title: When greedy stops working
rungs.purpose: Weights break every local rule. Keep the sort by end; replace the greedy choice with a max.

notes.weighted-job-scheduling: best[i] = max(best[i−1], w_i + best[p(i)]), with p(i) an upper bound over the sorted ends. Upper, so back-to-back bookings combine.

rungs.title: Extra practice
rungs.purpose: More interval sweeps — optional, counted only once started.

notes.max-population-year: Half-open lifetimes as +1/−1 events, and a prefix sum over the years.
notes.days-without-meetings: Merge, then count gaps in O(1) each — the calendar size never matters.
notes.meeting-rooms-iii: Free rooms by number, busy rooms by end time: two heaps for two orders.
notes.max-events-attended: Earliest deadline first: each day, attend the open event that closes soonest.
notes.data-stream-disjoint-intervals: Keep the intervals themselves and repair at most two neighbours per insert.
notes.teemo-attacking: Sorted equal-length intervals overlap only with neighbours: sum min(duration, gap).
notes.summary-ranges: Runs of consecutive values, found by comparing neighbours — in long, because the ints reach the extremes.
notes.remove-covered-intervals: Sort by start, ties by LONGER first; then one running max end decides coverage.
notes.video-stitching: Covering a range with the fewest intervals is Jump Game II over time.
notes.my-calendar: Accepted bookings never overlap, so only the two neighbours of a new one can clash.
notes.min-interval-per-query: Answer the queries in sorted order: intervals join a heap as they start and leave as they end.

units.build_it:
### The interval toolkit, from an empty file

Represent an interval as `int[]{start, end}`, half-open `[start, end)`, and keep
that convention for every function — then touching intervals do not overlap and
the length is simply `end − start`.

**1. `overlaps(a, b)`** and **`merge(list)`**. Test merge against a brute force
that paints a boolean timeline (times 0..30) and reads the blocks back.

**2. `insert(sorted, x)`** and **`subtract(sorted, x)`** — the three phases,
the second trimming instead of growing. Test both against the timeline painter.

**3. Peak concurrency three ways**: the ±1 sweep, the heap of ends, and the
timeline array. Stress-test all three against each other on random inputs with
many shared endpoints — that is where the tie rule matters.

**4. `maxNonOverlapping` by end**, and a brute force over subsets. Then add
weights and watch the greedy fail the stress test.

**5. Weighted scheduling** with the DP and a binary-searched predecessor. The
brute force from step 4 is its oracle. Get the predecessor boundary right on
intervals that touch — `[1, 3)` and `[3, 5)` are compatible.
units.next_up:
Order is done. The next stage looks inside the numbers themselves — their
factors, their remainders, their bits — and at grids, where the index
arithmetic is the whole problem.

invariant.statement: While merging intervals sorted by start: **`out` is a sorted list of disjoint blocks whose union is exactly the union of the intervals processed so far — and only the last block can overlap anything still to come.**
invariant.established: Before the first interval, `out` is empty and nothing has been processed; the union of nothing is empty.
invariant.maintained: The next interval `cur` starts at or after every processed start. So it cannot reach back past the last block's start into an earlier block — those all ended before the last block began. Either `cur` overlaps the last block, and extending that block's end to `max(end, cur.end)` covers exactly the new union; or it starts after the last block's end, and appending it as a new block keeps the list sorted and disjoint.
invariant.at_exit: After the last interval, `out` covers exactly the union of all of them, in sorted disjoint blocks — which is the answer, and also the input every “free time”, “covered length” and “subtract a range” question wants.
invariant.note: The phrase *only the last block can overlap* is what makes the pass linear. It holds only because of the sort by start — sort by end and it is false.

variants.name: Merge
variants.change: Sort by start; extend the last block or start a new one.
variants.when: Merge overlapping, union length, free time.
variants.gotcha: `max` on the end — the new interval may be nested inside the last.

variants.name: Insert into sorted
variants.change: Three loops: strictly before, overlapping (grow the new one), strictly after.
variants.when: Insert interval, subtract a range, add a booking.
variants.gotcha: The input is already sorted — re-sorting is a wasted O(n log n).

variants.name: Keep the most (sort by end)
variants.change: Keep an interval if it starts at or after the last kept end.
variants.when: Max non-overlapping, fewest removals.
variants.gotcha: Removals = n − kept. Sorting by start is the classic wrong answer.

variants.name: Stab with points
variants.change: Sort by end; shoot at the current end, skip everything it pierces.
variants.when: Minimum arrows, fewest points covering all intervals.
variants.gotcha: Touching counts as pierced here — `start <= arrow`, not `<`.

variants.name: Peak concurrency
variants.change: ±1 events sorted by time (ends before starts on ties), or a min-heap of ends.
variants.when: Meeting rooms, platforms, busiest moment, car pooling.
variants.gotcha: At equal timestamps, release before allocate.

variants.name: Two lists intersect
variants.change: Two pointers; emit `[max start, min end]`; advance the earlier end.
variants.when: Interval list intersections, common free time.
variants.gotcha: Advance by end, not by start.

variants.name: Greedy coverage
variants.change: Sort by start; among intervals starting within the covered prefix, take the one reaching furthest.
variants.when: Video stitching, minimum taps, jump game II in disguise.
variants.gotcha: A gap (no interval starts inside the covered prefix) means −1.

variants.name: Online (a sorted map)
variants.change: Keep intervals in a `TreeMap` by start; check `floorEntry` and `ceilingEntry`.
variants.when: My calendar, range modules, disjoint intervals from a stream.
variants.gotcha: Both neighbours must be checked — the previous one can reach past the new start.

variants.name: Weighted (DP)
variants.change: Sort by end; `best[i] = max(best[i-1], w_i + best[pred(i)])`, pred by binary search.
variants.when: Weighted job scheduling, max profit from non-overlapping jobs.
variants.gotcha: The predecessor search uses **ends ≤ start** — upper bound, not lower.

rewrites.title: Do any two meetings overlap?
rewrites.edit: The all-pairs check becomes a sort by start and one comparison per neighbour.
rewrites.why:
Once intervals are sorted by start, suppose `i < j` overlap but no adjacent pair
does. Interval `i + 1` starts at or after `i`, and does not overlap `i`, so it
starts at or after `i`'s end — and so does everything after it, including `j`.
Then `j` cannot overlap `i`. Contradiction: **some overlap implies an adjacent
overlap**.

So only n − 1 pairs need checking. The same argument, generalised, is why merge
only ever compares with the last block.

rewrites.title: Peak concurrency: a timeline, or events
rewrites.edit: Marking every time unit becomes sorting the 2n endpoints — the count only changes there.
rewrites.why:
Between two consecutive endpoints, nothing starts or ends, so the number of
active intervals is constant. The timeline array spends most of its work
re-reading that constant.

Sorting the events visits only the moments where the count changes, which makes
the cost independent of the time range — essential when times go to 10⁹. The
difference-array version (`+1` at start, `−1` at end, prefix-sum) is the middle
ground: O(n + T), fine when T is small.

The tie rule — `−1` before `+1` at the same time — encodes "a meeting ending at
2 does not clash with one starting at 2". Flip it and back-to-back meetings
count as overlapping.

rewrites.title: Insert without re-sorting
rewrites.edit: Re-sort-and-merge becomes three loops that exploit the order the input already has.
rewrites.why:
The re-sort discards a guarantee the input came with: sorted and disjoint. With
it, the intervals split into exactly three contiguous groups — entirely before
the new one, touching it, entirely after — and each group is one loop.

Only the middle group changes, and it collapses into the new interval by `min`
on the start and `max` on the end. Every interval is visited once, so the whole
insert is O(n), and there is no merge pass at all.

quizzes.prompt: For `[1, 10], [2, 3]` this outputs `[1, 3]`. Which change fixes it?
quizzes.answer: Extend with `last[1] = Math.max(last[1], cur[1])`
options: Sort by end instead of start
quizzes.why:
`[2, 3]` is **nested** inside `[1, 10]`. Overwriting the end shrinks the merged block
to `[1, 3]` and loses 3–10. The end of a merged block is the largest end seen, not
the latest.

quizzes.prompt: Back-to-back meetings `[0, 5)` and `[5, 10)` report 2 rooms. Which change fixes it?
quizzes.answer: At equal times sort `-1` first: `Integer.compare(x[1], y[1])`
options: At equal times sort `-1` first: `Integer.compare(x[1], y[1])`
Take the peak before adding the delta
quizzes.why:
The tie-break puts `+1` before `-1`, so at time 5 the new meeting is counted before
the old one releases its room: the count briefly reads 2. Ascending delta processes
ends first. (Moving ends to `end + 1` would make touching meetings overlap on
purpose — the opposite of what half-open intervals mean.)

quizzes.prompt: Intersecting two sorted interval lists, this misses some intersections. Which change fixes it?
quizzes.answer: Advance whichever interval ends first: `if (a[i][1] < b[j][1]) i++`
options: Advance whichever interval ends first: `if (a[i][1] < b[j][1]) i++`
Sort both lists by end first
quizzes.why:
The interval that ends first can meet nothing further in the other list; the one
that ends later might. Advancing by *start* can discard the long interval while it
still has intersections ahead — `a = [0, 10]`, `b = [1, 2], [5, 6]` loses `[5, 6]`.

quizzes.prompt: Closed intervals, touching ones merged. What does merging `[1, 4], [6, 8], [2, 3], [8, 9]` give?
quizzes.code:
Arrays.sort(iv, (x, y) -> Integer.compare(x[0], y[0]));
// extend the last block while cur[0] <= last[1], with max on the end
quizzes.why:
Sorted: `[1, 4], [2, 3], [6, 8], [8, 9]`. `[2, 3]` is nested (the max keeps 4),
`[6, 8]` starts a new block because 6 > 4, and `[8, 9]` touches it — `8 <= 8` — so
the block becomes `[6, 9]`.

quizzes.prompt: Balloons `[1, 6], [2, 8], [7, 12], [10, 16]`: sort by end and shoot at each unburst balloon's end. How many arrows?
quizzes.why:
The arrow at 6 bursts `[1, 6]` and `[2, 8]` (2 ≤ 6). `[7, 12]` starts after 6, so a
second arrow goes at 12 — bursting `[10, 16]` too. Two arrows.

quizzes.prompt: Weighted bookings: `[0, 5) w=1` and `[5, 10) w=1` should give 2, but this gives 1. Which change fixes it?
quizzes.answer: Use `upperBound` — bookings ending exactly at `start` are compatible
options: Use `upperBound` — bookings ending exactly at `start` are compatible
Sort by start instead of end
Take `best[i] = best[i - 1] + w` when they do not overlap
quizzes.why:
`lowerBound(ends, 5)` counts ends **< 5**, excluding `[0, 5)`, whose end is exactly
5 — yet a booking ending at 5 and one starting at 5 do not overlap. The compatible
prefix is the ends **≤ start**, which is the upper bound.

stuck.when: Sort by start, or by end?
stuck.ask: Building a union, merging, inserting: **start**. Keeping as many as possible, fewest removals, fewest arrows: **end**. How many at one moment: neither — events.

stuck.when: Do touching intervals overlap?
stuck.ask: Find the sentence in the statement; if it is silent, read the examples. Encode the answer in one comparison (`<` or `<=`) and use it everywhere.

stuck.when: There are too many pairs to compare
stuck.ask: After sorting by start, can an interval overlap anything except the block just before it? That is why one linear pass suffices.

stuck.when: I need “how many at the same time”
stuck.ask: Turn each interval into +1 at its start and −1 at its end. Sort the events (ends first on ties) and sweep a counter.

stuck.when: The intervals carry values or weights
stuck.ask: Greedy by end fails. Sort by end, DP over prefixes, and binary-search the last compatible interval.

stuck.when: Bookings arrive one at a time
stuck.ask: Keep a `TreeMap` by start. A new booking can only clash with its floor and ceiling neighbours — check those two.

edge_cases.breaks: Overwriting the end instead of taking the max.
Double-counting or dropping the shared point.
Processing starts before ends at equal times — it reports 2.
Keeping only one side of a block that should split in two.
Printing an empty line instead of `empty`.
A predecessor search that excludes an end equal to the start.

edge_cases.case: One heavy booking beats three light ones
edge_cases.breaks: Greedy by end time — it picks the three light ones.
A merge loop that only emits a block when the *next* interval starts.

walkthrough.title: Most Valuable Bookings — where greedy stops

steps.name: Read
steps.body:
*Requests `[s, e)` with payments w; accept non-overlapping ones to maximise the
total.* Touching is allowed. n up to 10⁵, so no subset enumeration.

steps.name: Route
steps.body:
It looks like the intervals router's "maximum non-overlapping" row — sort by end,
keep greedily. But that row's near miss is exactly this: **weights**. Maximising
the *count* and maximising the *weight* are different problems.

steps.name: Brute force
steps.body:
Try every subset and keep the best compatible one: O(2ⁿ · n). Then try the greedy
by end and find the counterexample: `[0, 10) w=100` against `[0, 2)`, `[2, 5)`,
`[5, 10)` at 30 each. Greedy keeps the three short ones (90); the answer is 100.

steps.name: Insight
steps.body:
Keep the sort by end — it still makes every compatible set a **prefix**. Let
`best[i]` be the best total using only the first i bookings. Booking i is either
skipped (`best[i − 1]`) or taken together with the best of the bookings that end at
or before its start. Those are a prefix of length p(i), found by binary search:

```
best[i] = max(best[i − 1], w_i + best[p(i)])
```

steps.name: Code
Test and price
steps.body:
- Back to back (`0 5 1 / 5 10 1 / 10 15 1`) → 3: checks the `<=` in the search.
- The heavy-versus-light case → 100: checks you did not fall back to greedy.
- Identical intervals → the heaviest one.

**Cost:** O(n log n) — the sort, plus one binary search per booking. Totals reach
10¹⁴: `long`.

stages.title: Numbers, Bits & Grids
stages.tagline: Look inside the values, and index the grid exactly.
stages.goal:
Up to here a number has been something to compare. This stage looks inside it.

**Number theory** is where an O(√n) or O(log n) idea replaces a loop over every
value — the first time the *size of a number* and the *size of the input* clearly
part ways — and where you learn to keep a huge count exact **modulo a prime**,
which every counting problem in the DP stage expects. **Bit manipulation** is the
same set of array patterns applied to 32 flags packed into one `int`, which is how
sets get represented when they have to be fast. **Simulation** needs no new idea
at all: only the index discipline that every grid problem in the trees-and-graphs
stage assumes you already have.

units.title: Math & Number Theory
units.tagline: Divisors, primes, gcd — and huge counts kept exact modulo a prime.
units.why:
Number-theory problems are the clearest example of the distinction that Big-O
makes and casual thinking does not: the difference between *how many numbers
you have* and *how large a number is*. Testing whether n is prime by trying
every candidate below it is O(n); stopping at √n is O(√n), and for n = 10⁹ that
is the difference between a billion operations and thirty thousand.

The two facts this unit is built on — trial division up to √n, and Euclid's
algorithm — carry a surprising amount of weight, and both have one-line proofs
worth knowing.

signals.why: Divisors pair up around the square root.
O(n log log n) beats n separate primality tests.
O(log n), and lcm follows from it.
Keeps everything inside `long` with no overflow.
Only valid for canonical systems — otherwise it is a DP problem.
O(log b); see the recursion unit.

signals.when: “number of ways to choose …”, many queries
signals.reach_for: Factorials and inverse factorials mod p
signals.why: O(N) once, then O(1) per C(n, r).

signals.when: A division inside a modular answer
signals.why: Only because p is prime — Fermat's little theorem.

skeletons.name: Trial division to √n
skeletons.when: Primality, divisor counting, divisor sums.
skeletons.note: `d * d <= n` keeps it in exact integer arithmetic.

skeletons.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
skeletons.when: Every prime below n, once.
skeletons.note: Start at `i * i`, and compute it in `long`.

skeletons.name: Euclid's gcd (and lcm)
skeletons.when: Fractions, common periods, array-wide gcd.
skeletons.code:
static long gcd(long a, long b) { return b == 0 ? a : gcd(b, a % b); }

long lcm = a / gcd(a, b) * b;      // divide FIRST to avoid overflow
skeletons.note: Fold with `g = gcd(g, x)` from 0 to get the gcd of a whole array.

skeletons.name: Greedy change with canonical coins
skeletons.when: US/EU denominations, where greedy is provably optimal.
skeletons.note: Valid only for canonical systems — `{1, 3, 4}` and amount 6 defeats it.

skeletons.name: Power and inverse modulo a prime
skeletons.when: a^b mod p, and division mod p.
skeletons.note: Reduce after every product; the product of two values below p always fits in a long.

skeletons.name: nCr modulo a prime
skeletons.when: Many binomial coefficients up to N.
skeletons.note: One O(log p) inverse; every other inverse factorial is a multiplication.

traces.title: Euclid's algorithm: gcd(1071, 462)
traces.intro: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)`, because anything dividing both a and b also divides the remainder. Stop when b reaches 0.
traces.takeaway: Three divisions from 1071 to the answer 21. The remainder is always smaller than b, and every two steps the numbers at least halve — that is the O(log min(a, b)) bound.

traces.title: Fast exponentiation: 3¹³ mod 1000
traces.intro: 13 is `1101` in binary, so 3¹³ = 3⁸ · 3⁴ · 3¹. Square the base each step; multiply it into the result only when the current low bit of the exponent is 1.
traces.takeaway: Four steps for a 4-bit exponent, and 3¹³ = 1 594 323, so the answer 323 checks out. Taking `% mod` after every multiplication is what keeps the numbers from overflowing on the way — the answer is the same either way, only the intermediate values differ.

pitfalls.symptom: 1 is reported as prime
pitfalls.cause: The `n < 2` guard is missing.
pitfalls.fix: Handle 0 and 1 before the loop; both are non-prime by definition.

pitfalls.symptom: The divisor count is one too high for perfect squares
pitfalls.cause: `d` and `n / d` are the same number when `d * d == n`, and both were counted.
pitfalls.fix: Add 1 rather than 2 in that case.

pitfalls.symptom: The sieve overflows or silently skips
pitfalls.cause: `i * i` computed in `int` wraps negative for i beyond ~46,340.
pitfalls.fix: Compute the inner start in `long`.

pitfalls.symptom: `lcm` overflows
pitfalls.cause: `a * b` was computed before dividing by the gcd.
pitfalls.fix: `a / gcd(a, b) * b` — the division is exact, so ordering is safe.

pitfalls.symptom: A modular result comes out negative
pitfalls.cause: Java's `%` keeps the sign of the left operand after a subtraction.
pitfalls.fix: `((x % MOD) + MOD) % MOD`.

pitfalls.symptom: Greedy change returns too many coins
pitfalls.cause: The denominations are not canonical, so greedy is not optimal.
pitfalls.fix: Use the coin-change DP from the DP unit.

pitfalls.symptom: A modular answer is wrong only on large inputs
pitfalls.cause: A product like `fact[n] * inv[r] * inv[n - r]` overflowed before the single `% MOD` at the end.
pitfalls.fix: Reduce after every multiplication: `fact[n] * inv[r] % MOD * inv[n - r] % MOD`.

pitfalls.symptom: `power(a, b)` is wrong for a near 10¹⁸
pitfalls.cause: The base was squared before being reduced, and `a * a` overflowed.
pitfalls.fix: `b %= MOD` first.

pitfalls.symptom: A division gives a wrong modular answer
pitfalls.cause: `(a / b) % MOD` was computed on already-reduced values, where integer division means nothing.
pitfalls.fix: Multiply by the modular inverse instead: `a * power(b, MOD - 2) % MOD`.

checks.q: Why is it enough to test divisors up to √n?
checks.a: Divisors pair as `d × n/d`, and in every pair one member is ≤ √n. A factor above √n therefore implies one below it, already tested.

checks.q: Why does the sieve's inner loop start at `i * i`?
checks.a: Every multiple `i·k` with `k < i` has a prime factor smaller than `i` and was crossed out when that factor was processed.

checks.q: Why is `gcd(a, b) == gcd(b, a % b)`?
checks.a: Any common divisor of `a` and `b` divides `a - qb = a % b`, and conversely, so the set of common divisors is unchanged. The remainder shrinks fast, giving O(log n).

checks.q: Why compute `lcm` as `a / gcd * b` rather than `a * b / gcd`?
checks.a: `a * b` can overflow before the division happens. Dividing first is exact because the gcd divides `a`.

checks.q: When is greedy coin change correct?
checks.a: Only for canonical denomination systems such as `{1, 5, 10, 25}`. For arbitrary coin sets it can be wrong, and dynamic programming is required.

checks.q: Why can two values below 10⁹ + 7 be multiplied in a `long` without overflow?
checks.a: Both are below 2³⁰, so the product is below 2⁶⁰ < 2⁶³. That is also why you must reduce after *each* multiplication — a third factor would not fit.

checks.q: How do you divide modulo a prime p?
checks.a: Multiply by the inverse. By Fermat's little theorem x^(p−1) ≡ 1, so x^(p−2) is x's inverse for any x not divisible by p.

checks.q: Given fact[] and invFact[N], how do you get every other invFact cheaply?
checks.a: Walk down: 1/(i−1)! = i · 1/i!, so invFact[i − 1] = invFact[i] · i mod p. One exponentiation instead of N.

bigo.why: If n has a factor above √n, it has a matching one below it, so trial division can stop at √n. `d * d <= n` avoids the floating-point `Math.sqrt` — keep `d` a `long` so the square cannot overflow.

The sieve of Eratosthenes: prime p crosses off n/p multiples, and summing n/p over primes gives n log log n — which is under 4n for any n you will meet. Starting at `p * p` is safe because smaller multiples were crossed off by smaller primes.
Euclid's algorithm: every two steps the smaller number at least halves. The worst case is consecutive Fibonacci numbers, and even for 64-bit values that is under 100 iterations.
Fast exponentiation squares the base and halves the exponent, so it takes one step per *bit* of e. 2⁶⁰ as an exponent is 60 multiplications instead of 10¹⁸.

Up to √i work for each of n numbers. (The precise count is a little lower — most composites exit on a tiny factor, leaving the primes to pay full price — but it grows far faster than the sieve.) Counting primes up to n is a sieve problem.

units.interview:
Pure number theory is rare in interviews, but √n and gcd show up as *steps*
inside larger problems — and the follow-up is always "why is that enough?".
Both proofs above are one sentence long, and being able to produce them
distinguishes someone who knows the trick from someone who knows why it works.

Modular arithmetic is the opposite: rarely the point, constantly required. A
counting solution that overflows on the large test is a failed solution, so
reduce after every operation without being asked.

rungs.title: Warm up
rungs.purpose: Divisibility, and a greedy that happens to be optimal.

notes.count-divisors: The √n loop, including the perfect-square case that is counted once, not twice.
notes.us-coins-change: Greedy works here because the denominations are canonical. Note *why*, because the coin-change DP later is the same problem without that property.

rungs.title: Core
rungs.purpose: Trial division and Euclid.

notes.is-prime: Guard `n < 2` first, then loop while `d * d <= n`.
notes.count-primes: The sieve: cross out multiples starting from p², and the whole range costs O(n log log n).

rungs.title: Counting modulo a prime
rungs.purpose: Reduce after every product, exponentiate by squaring, and divide by multiplying with an inverse.

notes.power-mod: Reduce the base before the first square — (10^18)² does not fit in a long.
notes.count-good-numbers: 5^even · 4^odd, with exponents near 10^15: two power-mods and one product, reduced.
notes.ncr-mod-queries: Factorials once, one Fermat inverse at the top, the rest walking down. Then each query is three lookups.

rungs.title: Extra practice
rungs.purpose: Batch versions of the same two ideas — more reps, no new idea.

notes.gcd-of-array: A fold. `gcd(0, x) == x` makes 0 the right starting accumulator.
notes.excel-column-number: Base 26 read left to right — with digits 1 to 26 and no zero.
notes.multiply-strings: Grade-school multiplication where the shift is index arithmetic: i + j + 1.
notes.excel-column-title: Base 26 with digits 1..26 and no zero: subtract one before each remainder.
notes.nth-digit: Skip whole blocks of equal-length numbers with arithmetic, then index into one number.
notes.fraction-to-recurring-decimal: Long division has one piece of state — the remainder — so a repeat marks the period.
notes.smallest-repunit-divisible-by-k: Carry only the remainder; k states mean a repeat within k steps proves 'never'.

units.next_up: One more representation to go: the bits an integer is actually made of.

units.title: Bit Manipulation
units.tagline: 32 flags in one int, and the XOR trick that cancels pairs.
units.why:
An `int` is 32 booleans. Once you see it that way, a set of up to 32 elements
becomes a single number you can compare, hash, store in an array and pass
around for free — which is the foundation of bitmask dynamic programming later,
and the reason subset enumeration is written the way it is.

The immediate payoff is smaller and sharper: **XOR cancels pairs**. Problems
that look like they need a hash map — "every element appears twice except one" —
collapse to a single accumulator and O(1) space.
units.model:
### The operators

| Expression | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `a & b` | 1 where **both** are 1 — masking, testing |
| `a \| b` | 1 where **either** is 1 — setting |
| `a ^ b` | 1 where they **differ** — toggling, cancelling |
| `~a` | flip every bit |
| `a << k` | multiply by 2ᵏ |
| `a >> k` | divide by 2ᵏ, **sign-extending** |
| `a >>> k` | divide by 2ᵏ, shifting in zeros |

### The four idioms

```java
boolean isSet = (x & (1 << i)) != 0;   // test bit i
x |= (1 << i);                         // set bit i
x &= ~(1 << i);                        // clear bit i
x ^= (1 << i);                         // toggle bit i
```

### Why XOR is special

Three properties, and every XOR trick follows from them:

- `x ^ x == 0` — a value cancels itself
- `x ^ 0 == x` — zero is the identity
- it is commutative and associative — **order does not matter**

So XOR-ing an entire array where every value appears twice except one leaves
exactly the odd one out. Same idea for the missing number in `0…n`: XOR the
indices and the values together and everything pairs off but the absentee.

### Two more worth memorising

```java
x & (x - 1)     // clears the lowest set bit
x & -x          // isolates the lowest set bit
```

`x & (x - 1) == 0` tests for a power of two (plus a `x > 0` guard, because 0
passes and is not one). Repeatedly clearing the lowest set bit counts the bits
in O(number of set bits) — Kernighan's algorithm.

### Counting bits for every number

`countBits[i] = countBits[i >> 1] + (i & 1)`: i without its last bit, plus that
bit. That is a one-line DP, and it is the bridge to the DP stage.

### The traps

Shifts on `int` use only the low 5 bits of the count, so `1 << 32` is `1`, not
0. Use `1L << k` whenever k can reach 32. And `>>` sign-extends, so a negative
value shifted right stays negative forever — use `>>>` when you are treating
the int as raw bits.

signals.why: Pairs cancel; the survivor is the answer. O(1) space.
Or use the sum formula — XOR cannot overflow.
Clears one set bit per iteration.
A power of two has exactly one set bit.
Each mask is one subset; bit i means element i is in.

signals.when: “for every i from 0 to n, count bits”
signals.why: One pass, and your first DP recurrence.

skeletons.name: XOR fold
skeletons.when: The unpaired element; the missing number.
skeletons.code:
int x = 0;
for (int v : a) x ^= v;      // pairs cancel, the loner remains
skeletons.note: For “missing from 0…n”, also XOR in every index.

skeletons.name: Kernighan bit count
skeletons.when: Population count, Hamming weight.
skeletons.code:
int count = 0;
while (x != 0) { x &= (x - 1); count++; }   // clears the lowest set bit
skeletons.note: Loops once per *set* bit, not once per bit.

skeletons.name: Test / set / clear
skeletons.when: Using an int as a set of up to 32 elements.
skeletons.note: `1L << i` when i may reach 32 or beyond.

skeletons.name: Enumerate all subsets
skeletons.when: Brute force over subsets when n ≤ ~20.
skeletons.note: 2ⁿ · n total. The backtracking unit builds the same subsets recursively.

traces.title: Counting set bits by clearing the lowest one: x = 44
traces.intro: `x − 1` flips the lowest set bit to 0 and every 0 below it to 1. ANDing with x keeps everything above that bit and clears the rest.
traces.takeaway: 44 is `00101100`: three set bits, three iterations — the loop never visits the five zero bits. The same expression `x & (x − 1)` being 0 is the power-of-two test.

traces.title: The element that appears once: XOR of [4, 1, 2, 1, 2]
traces.intro: XOR is its own inverse (`v ^ v == 0`) and order does not matter, so every pair cancels no matter where its two halves sit.
traces.takeaway: The accumulator ends at 4 — the unpaired value — after passing through states like `111` (7) that mean nothing on their own. One pass, O(1) space, no set.

costs.note: Beats a hash map's O(n) space.

pitfalls.symptom: `1 << 32` gives 1 instead of 0
pitfalls.cause: Java masks the shift count to 5 bits for `int` (6 for `long`).
pitfalls.fix: Use `1L << k` whenever k can reach 32.

pitfalls.symptom: A right shift of a negative number never reaches 0
pitfalls.cause: `>>` sign-extends, so the sign bit keeps refilling.
pitfalls.fix: Use `>>>` when treating the value as raw bits.

pitfalls.symptom: A test of `x & mask == 0` behaves oddly
pitfalls.cause: `==` binds tighter than `&` in Java, so it parses as `x & (mask == 0)`.
pitfalls.fix: Parenthesise: `(x & mask) == 0`.

pitfalls.symptom: 0 is reported as a power of two
pitfalls.cause: `(x & (x - 1)) == 0` is true for 0.
pitfalls.fix: Add the `x > 0` guard.

pitfalls.symptom: XOR gives the wrong answer when values repeat three times
pitfalls.cause: XOR cancels *pairs*; a triple leaves one copy behind.
pitfalls.fix: Use counting (or bitwise counts mod 3) when the multiplicity is not two.

checks.q: Why does XOR-ing an array where every value appears twice leave the loner?
checks.a: XOR is commutative and associative and `x ^ x == 0`, so order is irrelevant and every pair annihilates, leaving `0 ^ loner`.

checks.q: What does `x & (x - 1)` do, and what does it test?
checks.a: It clears the lowest set bit. Being 0 afterwards means x had exactly one set bit — a power of two, given `x > 0`.

checks.q: Why is `1 << 32` equal to 1 in Java?
checks.a: Shift counts on `int` are taken modulo 32, so 32 becomes 0. Use `1L << 32`.

checks.q: Explain `dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1)`.
checks.a: `i >> 1` is i without its lowest bit — a smaller, already-computed value — and `i & 1` adds that bit back. It is a recurrence, i.e. dynamic programming.

bigo.why: 2ⁿ subsets, n bits checked in each. Reusing `sum[mask ^ lowestBit]` computes each subset sum in O(1) and brings it to O(2ⁿ) — the same trick as a running prefix.
One pass, O(1) extra space. Pairs cancel under XOR in any order, so what remains is the element that appears an odd number of times — no hash set needed.

Kernighan's trick removes one set bit per iteration, so the loop runs once per 1-bit rather than once per bit position. For an `int` that is at most 32 either way — `Integer.bitCount` is the O(1) library call.

Every (mask, submask) pair is visited once, and each element is in one of three states — not in mask, in mask but not sub, in both — so there are 3ⁿ pairs. It is far less than the 4ⁿ the two nested exponentials suggest.

bigo.code: boolean powerOfTwo = x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0;
bigo.why: A power of two has a single set bit, and `x − 1` flips it and every bit below, so the AND is zero exactly then. A loop that halves x would be O(log x).

units.interview:
Bit tricks are a bonus, not a core competency: the wrong move is opening with
one where a hash map is clearer. The right move is offering it as the follow-up
— *"if you want O(1) space and each value appears exactly twice, XOR does it"* —
and being able to say why the algebra works.

rungs.title: Core
rungs.purpose: XOR as a cancelling accumulator.

notes.missing-number: Two solutions: the sum formula and the XOR fold. XOR cannot overflow, which is the argument for it.

rungs.title: Stretch

notes.add-binary: Schoolbook addition in base 2. The final carry is the classic bug.
notes.reverse-bits: Shift out of one end and into the other, thirty-two times.
notes.sum-two-integers-bits: XOR is addition without carries; AND shifted left is the carries. Repeat until none remain.
notes.hamming-distance: XOR marks where two numbers differ; v & (v − 1) counts the marks.
notes.bitwise-and-of-range: Only the common binary prefix of the two ends survives counting between them.
notes.single-number-ii: XOR cancels pairs; summing each bit column modulo 3 cancels triples.
notes.max-product-word-lengths: A set of 26 letters is a 26-bit integer, and disjointness is one AND.
notes.xor-queries-subarray: XOR is its own inverse, so prefix XOR answers range queries like prefix sums.
notes.number-complement: A mask exactly as wide as the number flips only its meaningful bits.

units.next_up:
One unit left in this stage, and it introduces no new technique at all — only
the index discipline that grid problems demand.

units.title: Simulation & Matrices
units.tagline: Follow the rules exactly, on a grid, without breaking your own indices.
units.why:
Some problems have no trick. They describe a process — a robot walking, cells
updating, a matrix rotating — and the work is to execute it *exactly*, which is
harder than it sounds because the failure mode is subtle: you overwrite a value
you still needed, or you update a cell and then read it again in the same step.

This unit is also where 2-D index arithmetic becomes automatic. The neighbour
loop, the bounds check and the transpose-then-reverse identity are the
vocabulary that every grid traversal in stage 6 assumes you already have.
units.model:
### Grid vocabulary

```java
int rows = g.length, cols = g[0].length;

int[][] DIRS = {{-1,0},{1,0},{0,-1},{0,1}};        // 4-directional
for (int[] d : DIRS) {
    int ni = i + d[0], nj = j + d[1];
    if (ni < 0 || ni >= rows || nj < 0 || nj >= cols) continue;   // bounds FIRST
    ...
}
```

The bounds check comes **before** the read, always. Eight neighbours is the same
loop with `{-1,0,1} × {-1,0,1}` minus the `(0,0)` centre.

### The in-place trap

When the update rule reads neighbours, updating a cell immediately corrupts the
reads of its neighbours. Three ways out, in increasing order of cleverness:

1. **Write to a copy**, then swap. Always correct, costs O(n·m).
2. **Two passes with an encoding**: store both old and new state in one cell
   (e.g. old value + 2 × new value), then divide out on a second pass. O(1)
   extra space.
3. **Mark in the margins**: use row 0 and column 0 as flags, as in
   `set-matrix-zeroes`. Cheapest and the easiest to get wrong.

Start with the copy. Do the clever version only when asked for O(1) space, and
say why it works before you write it.

### Rotation

Rotating a square matrix 90° clockwise:

```
transpose (swap a[i][j] with a[j][i], j > i)  →  reverse each row
```

Writing the two-step identity down is far more reliable than trying to derive
`a[j][n-1-i]` under pressure.

### Spiral traversal

Keep four boundaries — `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right` — walk one edge, then
move that boundary inward. The subtlety is that after the top row and right
column, you must re-check `top <= bottom` and `left <= right` before walking
back, or a single remaining row is emitted twice.

### Rotating an array by k

Three reversals: reverse the whole thing, reverse the first k, reverse the rest.
O(1) space and no modular index juggling. Normalise `k %= n` first, or the
reversal bounds go out of range.

signals.reach_for: Copy, or encode two states in one cell
signals.why: Simultaneous updates cannot be done in place naively.
Two simple steps beat one hard index formula.
Re-check the bounds between the two return edges.
O(1) space; normalise `k %= n` first.
Same loop for 4- and 8-connectivity.
States repeat; simulating 10⁹ steps directly will not finish.

skeletons.name: Neighbour scan
skeletons.when: Counting mines, flood fills, any adjacency rule.
skeletons.note: Bounds before access, every time. This exact loop reappears in every grid BFS.

skeletons.name: Simultaneous update via a copy
skeletons.when: Game of Life and every “all cells update at once” rule.
skeletons.note: Correct by construction. Optimise to in-place encoding only if asked.

skeletons.name: Rotate 90° clockwise
skeletons.when: Square matrix rotation, in place.
skeletons.note: `j = i + 1` — transposing the whole square swaps everything back.

skeletons.name: Rotate an array by k
skeletons.when: Cyclic shift, O(1) space.
skeletons.note: Without `k %= n` the second reversal can run off the end.

skeletons.name: Spiral boundaries
skeletons.when: Spiral order, layer-by-layer traversal.
skeletons.note: The two guarded edges are where single-row and single-column matrices break.

traces.title: Rotating a matrix 90° clockwise in place
traces.intro: Rotation is two reflections: flip across the main diagonal, then flip each row left-to-right. Neither step needs a second matrix.
traces.takeaway: The first column read bottom-up, `7 4 1`, has become the first row — which is what a clockwise turn does. Reversing each *column* instead of each row gives the counter-clockwise rotation. The transpose loop starts `j` at `i + 1`; starting at 0 swaps every pair twice and undoes itself.

costs.note: Versus O(n) extra with a buffer.

pitfalls.symptom: `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at an edge cell
pitfalls.cause: A neighbour was read before its coordinates were bounds-checked.
pitfalls.fix: Check `ni`/`nj` first, then access.

pitfalls.symptom: The simulation drifts after the first step
pitfalls.cause: Cells were updated in place, so later cells read already-updated neighbours.
pitfalls.fix: Write into a copy, or encode old and new state in the same cell.

pitfalls.symptom: The rotated matrix is a mirror image
pitfalls.cause: The transpose loop ran over all `j` rather than `j > i`, swapping twice.
pitfalls.fix: Start the inner loop at `i + 1`.

pitfalls.symptom: Spiral order repeats the middle row
pitfalls.cause: The bottom and left edges were walked without re-checking the shrunk bounds.
pitfalls.fix: Guard both return edges with `if (top <= bot)` and `if (left <= right)`.

pitfalls.symptom: Rotating by k crashes or does nothing
pitfalls.cause: `k` was larger than `n`, or negative.
pitfalls.fix: `k = ((k % n) + n) % n` before the reversals.

pitfalls.symptom: Simulating a huge step count times out
pitfalls.cause: The process was executed literally when it is eventually periodic.
pitfalls.fix: Detect the repeated state and jump ahead by whole cycles.

checks.q: Why can Game of Life not be updated in place naively?
checks.a: The rule reads a cell's neighbours; overwriting a cell makes later cells read the new value instead of the old. Every cell must see the same generation.

checks.q: Give the two-step identity for a 90° clockwise rotation.
checks.a: Transpose (swap `a[i][j]` with `a[j][i]` for `j > i`), then reverse each row.

checks.q: Why does rotating an array by k use three reversals?
checks.a: Reversing the whole array puts the last k elements at the front but backwards; reversing each of the two blocks restores their internal order. O(1) space.

checks.q: What breaks in a spiral traversal of a single-row matrix?
checks.a: Without re-checking `top <= bot` before the bottom edge, the same row is emitted twice — once left-to-right, once right-to-left.

bigo.why: Transpose then reverse each row: each cell is touched a constant number of times. For a matrix, n² is *linear in the input* — it is the number of cells.
Schoolbook matrix multiplication: n² output cells, each a dot product of length n. Swapping the loop order to i-k-j keeps it O(n³) but is several times faster, because it walks memory in order.

Every generation touches every cell, and each cell looks at a constant 8 neighbours. Simulation cost is steps × state size, and the step count usually comes from the input — read it off the constraints before you simulate.
Spiral order visits every cell exactly once. The outer `while` runs min(r, c)/2 times, but multiplying it by the inner loops double-counts — count the cells emitted.
The loop runs T times, and `ArrayList.remove(0)` shifts every remaining element. Simulating a queue with a list turns an O(T) simulation into O(T·n); an `ArrayDeque` makes each step O(1).

units.interview:
Simulation questions look easy and eliminate people, because the grader is
exact and the specification has more cases than it first appears. The winning
approach is visible discipline: restate the rule, name the update order,
enumerate the edge cases (first row, last column, 1×n grid), *then* type. And
when asked for O(1) space, explain the encoding before writing it.

units.next_up:
Every technique so far has worked on data laid out in a line. The next stage
introduces structures that impose their own shape — and with it, their own
operations.

stages.title: Linear Data Structures
stages.tagline: Pick the container whose costs match the question.
stages.goal:
Every structure here is a deliberate trade. A stack gives up random access and
gets perfect nesting. A deque gives up the middle and gets both ends. A linked
list gives up indexing and gets O(1) insertion. A heap gives up total order and
gets the minimum for almost nothing.

The recurring exam question is therefore not "how does a heap work?" but
**"which one, and what does it cost?"** — and the design unit at the end of the
curriculum is that question asked a dozen different ways.

| Structure | O(1) | O(log n) | O(n) | Java |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Array | index, append\* | — | insert, search | `int[]`, `ArrayList` |
| Stack | push, pop, peek | — | search | `ArrayDeque` |
| Queue / Deque | add/remove at **either** end | — | search, index | `ArrayDeque` |
| Linked list | insert/delete at a **known** node | — | index, search | hand-rolled |
| Heap | peek min | push, pop | search, arbitrary delete | `PriorityQueue` |
| Hash map | get, put | — | (worst case only) | `HashMap` |

\* amortised — see the stacks unit's internals for what that word is buying.

Each unit here also asks you to **build the structure once**, from scratch, on
a plain array. That is not ceremony: until you have written the sift-down loop
or the ring buffer's wrap-around, its cost is a fact you memorised rather than
one you can re-derive at a whiteboard.

units.title: Stacks & Monotonic Stacks
units.tagline: Last in, first out — and the trick that makes “next greater” linear.
units.why:
A stack is the right structure whenever the most recent unfinished thing is the
one you need next. Bracket matching is the obvious case; the important one is
the **monotonic stack**, which answers *"for each element, what is the next
larger one to its right?"* in a single pass instead of n scans.

That pattern is worth real effort. It is the difference between O(n²) and O(n)
on a whole family of Medium and Hard problems — daily temperatures, stock
spans, histogram rectangles — and all of them are the same fifteen lines with
one comparison changed.
units.model:
### The structure

Push, pop, peek — all O(1), all at one end.

```java
Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
st.push(x);  st.peek();  st.pop();  st.isEmpty();
```

### Matching and nesting

A stack *is* a nesting checker. Push openers, and on a closer check that the
top is its partner:

```java
for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
    if (isOpen(c)) st.push(c);
    else if (st.isEmpty() || !matches(st.pop(), c)) return false;
}
return st.isEmpty();      // leftovers mean unclosed brackets
```

Both failure modes matter: a closer with an empty stack, and a non-empty stack
at the end. Forgetting the second is the classic half-right solution.

### The monotonic stack

Keep the stack **sorted by construction** — here, decreasing — and store
*indices*, not values:

```java
Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();          // indices, values decreasing
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    while (!st.isEmpty() && a[st.peek()] < a[i]) {
        int j = st.pop();
        res[j] = i - j;         // a[i] is the next greater element for index j
    }
    st.push(i);
}
```

The insight to internalise: **when you pop something, you have just found its
answer.** An element sits on the stack precisely while its answer is still
unknown; the moment something bigger arrives, it is resolved and leaves. The
trace below is that sentence, executed.

Cost is O(n) despite the nested `while`, for the same amortised reason as the
sliding window: every index is pushed once and popped at most once.

Change the comparison and you change the question:

| Comparison in the `while` | Answers |
| --- | --- |
| `a[st.peek()] < a[i]` | next **greater** to the right |
| `a[st.peek()] > a[i]` | next **smaller** to the right |
| iterate right-to-left | the same two questions, to the **left** |

### Histogram rectangles

The hardest common application, and it is the same loop: while the stack's top
bar is taller than the current one, pop it and compute the rectangle whose
height is that bar — its width running from the new stack top up to the current
index, **exclusive at both ends**. Push a sentinel height of 0 at the end and
every remaining bar is flushed with no special-case code.
units.internals:
### What is under `ArrayDeque`

A plain `Object[]` plus two indices, used as a **ring buffer**. Pushing writes
at one index and steps it; popping reads and steps back. No node is allocated,
nothing is linked, and both operations are a couple of array accesses — which
is why "O(1)" here really is a handful of instructions rather than a pointer
chase through memory.

When the array fills, it allocates one of double the size and copies. That copy
is O(n), so a single push can be expensive — but it happens only after n cheap
ones, and doubling means the total copying across n pushes is
`n/2 + n/4 + … < n`. Spread over the pushes, the cost per push is constant.
That is what **amortised O(1)** means, and it is the same argument the
monotonic stack's `while` loop uses; being able to give it in one sentence is
worth more than the code.

### The Java toolbox

| Want | Use | Not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A stack | `ArrayDeque` (`push`/`pop`/`peek`) | `Stack` — see below |
| A stack of primitives, hot loop | `int[] st; int top = -1;` | boxing every value |
| Fixed, known capacity | a plain array + a `top` index | anything with a header |

**Never `java.util.Stack`.** It extends `Vector`, so every method is
synchronised (a lock you are not using, on every single operation), and — the
part that actually causes bugs — **it iterates bottom-to-top**, the opposite of
`ArrayDeque`. Code that prints a `Stack` gets the reverse of what the author
expected. It survives only for compatibility.

`ArrayDeque` also **rejects `null`**, because `null` is its "empty" signal from
`peek()`/`poll()`. That is a feature: it turns "I stored a null" into an
immediate `NullPointerException` at the `push` rather than a mystery later.

### The stack you did not declare

The **call stack** is this structure — one frame pushed per call, popped on
return. That is why recursion depth is a memory cost (the recursion unit), and why *any*
recursion can be rewritten with an explicit stack: you are just taking over the
bookkeeping the JVM was doing. When a recursive DFS overflows on 10⁵ nodes,
that rewrite is the fix.

signals.why: Push openers, match on closers, require empty at the end.
Pop when something bigger arrives; the popped element's answer is now known.
Same loop; the surviving stack top is the previous smaller element.
Each popped bar is the limiting height of a rectangle.
Back-and-forward is one stack per direction.
Nesting again — the parser's shape.

signals.when: Recursive DFS that overflows the stack
signals.reach_for: The same DFS with an explicit stack
signals.why: You take over the bookkeeping the call stack was doing.

traces.title: Monotonic stack on [73, 74, 72, 76]
traces.intro: “Days until a warmer temperature.” The stack holds indices whose answer is still unknown, top first. Watch the pops: every pop writes one answer.
traces.takeaway: Four indices pushed, three popped, one left over — seven operations for n = 4. The `while` never makes it quadratic because nothing is pushed twice.

traces.title: Histogram widths on heights [2, 1, 5, 6, 2]
traces.intro: The confusing part is never the popping — it is the width. After popping bar `j`, the rectangle of height `h[j]` extends from just after the NEW stack top to just before `i`: width = `i − left − 1`.
traces.takeaway: The winner (10) is a bar of height 5 spanning two columns — a rectangle that belongs to no single bar's own width, which is exactly why the naive per-bar expansion is O(n²) and this is not.

pitfalls.symptom: “Valid” is returned for a string with unclosed brackets
pitfalls.cause: The final `st.isEmpty()` check is missing.
pitfalls.fix: Leftovers on the stack mean unmatched openers — the answer is false.

pitfalls.symptom: `NoSuchElementException` from `pop`
pitfalls.cause: A closer arrived with an empty stack.
pitfalls.fix: Test `isEmpty()` before every pop.

pitfalls.symptom: The monotonic stack gives values but you need distances
pitfalls.cause: Values were pushed instead of indices.
pitfalls.fix: Push indices; read the value as `a[st.peek()]`.

pitfalls.symptom: The answer is missing for the last few elements
pitfalls.cause: Elements still on the stack at the end were never resolved.
pitfalls.fix: Either handle the leftovers explicitly or push a sentinel that flushes them.

pitfalls.symptom: Iterating a stack prints it upside down
pitfalls.cause: The legacy `Stack` extends `Vector` and iterates bottom-to-top.
pitfalls.fix: Use `ArrayDeque`, whose iterator runs top-to-bottom.

pitfalls.symptom: `NullPointerException` on `push`
pitfalls.cause: `ArrayDeque` rejects `null`, because `null` is its empty signal.
pitfalls.fix: Push a sentinel object or an index instead of a null.

pitfalls.symptom: Duplicate heights are counted twice in the histogram
pitfalls.cause: The comparison used `>` where `>=` was needed (or vice versa).
pitfalls.fix: Decide how ties are handled and keep the comparison consistent; with `>=` an equal bar is popped early and the later one recovers the full width.

checks.q: Why is a monotonic-stack pass O(n) when it contains a `while` loop?
checks.a: Each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so the total number of inner iterations across the whole run is at most n.

checks.q: What does it mean, semantically, when an element is popped?
checks.a: Its answer has just been found. Elements remain on the stack only while their next-greater (or next-smaller) element is still unknown.

checks.q: What is `ArrayDeque` actually made of, and what does “amortised” buy?
checks.a: An `Object[]` ring buffer with two indices. When it fills it doubles and copies — O(n) once, after n cheap pushes, so the cost spread over all pushes is constant.

checks.q: Why `ArrayDeque` instead of `Stack` in Java?
checks.a: `Stack` extends `Vector`: synchronised on every call, slower, and it iterates bottom-to-top, which is rarely what the author meant.

checks.q: In bracket matching, what do leftovers on the stack mean?
checks.a: Openers that were never closed — the string is invalid, even though no mismatch was ever detected during the scan.

checks.q: After popping bar j in the histogram, why is the width `i − left − 1` rather than `i − j`?
checks.a: Bar j's rectangle extends left past j, over every bar already popped because it was taller. The new stack top is the first bar too short to be included, so the span is everything strictly between it and i.

bigo.why: One push or pop per character, each O(1). The stack is what lets you match without rescanning — a count would do for one bracket type, but not for three.
The monotonic stack. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the inner `while` does at most n pops over the whole run. It looks quadratic and is linear.
Next-greater by scanning ahead. The `break` helps on random data and not at all on a decreasing array, where every scan runs to the end. That worst case is the one the monotonic stack fixes.

`Stack.search` is a linear scan from the top. A stack answers "what is on top?" in O(1) and "is x anywhere in here?" in O(n) — use a set beside it for the second. (And prefer `ArrayDeque`: `Stack` is synchronised legacy.)
Each push records the minimum *as of that height*, so `getMin` is a peek: O(1). Paying O(1) extra space per element to avoid an O(n) scan per query is the whole min-stack idea.

units.interview:
The monotonic stack is one of the few patterns an interviewer will accept as a
complete answer the moment you name it — but only with the amortisation
argument attached. "Each index enters and leaves the stack once, so the pass is
O(n)" is the sentence. Without it, the nested `while` reads as O(n²) and you
will be asked to defend it anyway. The same sentence, in its other form —
"`ArrayDeque` doubles and copies, so push is amortised O(1)" — is the answer to
the follow-up about the structure itself.

units.build_it:
**Write a stack on a raw array.** `int[] data; int top = -1;` with `push`, `pop`,
`peek` and `isEmpty` — twenty lines, no generics, no library.

Then make it grow: when `top + 1 == data.length`, allocate `data.length * 2` and
`System.arraycopy`. Now add a counter for elements copied, push a million values,
and print it. You will get **fewer than two million copies for a million pushes**
— under two per push, no matter how large n gets. That number is what "amortised
O(1)" means, and having produced it yourself is why you will still be able to
explain it under pressure.

Then try growth by `+1` instead of `×2` and watch the counter become ~n²/2.
units.next_up:
A stack reverses the order things arrive in. The next structure preserves it —
and then, by opening its other end, does something a stack cannot.

units.title: Queues & Deques
units.tagline: First in, first out — and the deque that answers “max of every window”.
units.why:
A stack hands back the most recent item. A **queue** hands back the oldest, and
that single difference is the whole reason BFS finds shortest paths: processing
in arrival order means processing in distance order. Every graph traversal in
stage 6 runs on this structure, so the cost of getting it wrong compounds.

A **deque** — a double-ended queue — opens both ends, and unlocks the pattern
this unit exists for: the **monotonic deque**, which gives you the maximum of
every sliding window in O(n) total. It is the direct sequel to the monotonic
stack, with one addition: elements now also expire from the *front* because
they have fallen out of the window.
units.model:
### One class, three roles

`ArrayDeque` is a stack, a queue and a deque depending on which methods you
call. Pick one vocabulary per use and stay in it:

| Role | Add | Remove | Inspect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Stack** (LIFO) | `push` | `pop` | `peek` |
| **Queue** (FIFO) | `offer` / `addLast` | `poll` / `pollFirst` | `peekFirst` |
| **Deque** | `offerFirst` / `offerLast` | `pollFirst` / `pollLast` | `peekFirst` / `peekLast` |

Mixing `push` (which adds at the **front**) with `poll` (which removes from the
front) silently gives you a stack when you wanted a queue. If BFS returns a
non-shortest path, this is the first thing to check.

### The queue, in BFS

```java
Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
q.offer(src);
while (!q.isEmpty()) {
    int u = q.poll();
    for (int v : adj(u)) if (!seen[v]) { seen[v] = true; q.offer(v); }
}
```

Arrival order is distance order — that is the entire justification for BFS's
shortest-path property, and it is a property of the *queue*, not of the graph.

### The monotonic deque

Keep the deque holding indices whose values are **decreasing**. Then the front
is always the maximum of the current window:

```java
Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();          // indices, values decreasing
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() <= i - k) dq.pollFirst();   // expired
    while (!dq.isEmpty() && a[dq.peekLast()] <= a[i]) dq.pollLast(); // dominated
    dq.offerLast(i);
    if (i >= k - 1) out[i - k + 1] = a[dq.peekFirst()];
}
```

Two evictions, for two different reasons, and confusing them is the bug:

- **From the front — expiry.** That index has left the window. It is about
  *position*.
- **From the back — domination.** A new element that is larger *and* newer makes
  everything smaller behind it permanently useless: it will leave the window
  later and it is bigger now, so no future window can ever prefer them. It is
  about *value*.

That domination argument is the one to say aloud. It is why the answer is always
at the front, and why the structure never needs to look at its middle.

Still O(n): every index is added once and removed once, by exactly one of the
two rules.

### Circular buffers

A queue on a fixed array wraps around:

```java
int[] buf = new int[cap]; int head = 0, size = 0;
void offer(int x) { buf[(head + size) % cap] = x; size++; }
int  poll()       { int x = buf[head]; head = (head + 1) % cap; size--; return x; }
```

Keep an explicit `size`. The tempting alternative — two indices and "empty when
`head == tail`" — cannot distinguish empty from full, since both look identical.
The classic workarounds are a `size` field or leaving one slot permanently
unused; the field is clearer.

### A queue of timestamps

"How many events in the last five minutes" is a queue used as a **sliding
window over time**: append each event, then drop from the front while the front
is older than the cutoff. Every event is added once and dropped once, so despite
the inner `while` the whole thing is amortised O(1) per query.
units.internals:
### The ring buffer

`ArrayDeque` is an `Object[]` with a `head` and a `tail` index, and it is
*circular*: when an index runs off the end it wraps to 0. That is the whole
trick, and it is why adding at the front is as cheap as adding at the back —
"the front" is just wherever `head` currently points, not physical slot 0.

Java sizes the array to a power of two so the wrap is a bit-mask,
`(i + 1) & (capacity - 1)`, rather than a `%` — division is far slower than a
mask, and this runs on every single operation. When it fills, it doubles and
copies, giving the same amortised O(1) as the stack.

### Why never `LinkedList` as a queue

`LinkedList` implements `Queue`, so it compiles and it works, and it is still
the wrong answer:

| | `ArrayDeque` | `LinkedList` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Per element | one array slot | a **node object**: header, value, two pointers |
| Memory | ~1 reference | ~4-6× that |
| Locality | contiguous — cache-friendly | scattered — a cache miss per step |
| Allocation | one array, rarely | one object per `offer`, plus GC pressure |

Same O(1) on paper; several times slower in practice, which is exactly the case
where Big-O has to be supplemented with "and the constant matters".

### The Java toolbox

| Want | Use | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FIFO queue | `ArrayDeque` via `Queue` | `offer` / `poll` / `peek` |
| Both ends | `ArrayDeque` via `Deque` | `First` / `Last` suffixes throughout |
| Fixed capacity, no allocation | `int[]` + head + size | the circular buffer above |
| Priority order, not arrival order | `PriorityQueue` | a heap — next unit; **not** FIFO |
| Blocking / cross-thread | `ArrayBlockingQueue` | outside this curriculum |

Two API traps. The `add`/`remove`/`element` family **throws** on an empty or
full queue; the `offer`/`poll`/`peek` family returns `false`/`null` instead.
Prefer the second and check the result. And `ArrayDeque` forbids `null`, for
the same reason the stack does: `null` is the "nothing there" answer from
`poll`.

`PriorityQueue` also implements `Queue`, so a misplaced import gives you a
structure that compiles as a queue and delivers in *sorted* order — a BFS that
returns wrong distances with no error anywhere.
